"onward to and into (a place); as far as, all the way to; up to the time of;" mid-13c., perhaps a modification of until, with southern to in place of northern equivalent till. Or perhaps a contraction of native *und to, formed on the model of until from Old English *un- "up to, as far as," cognate of the first element in until.
"Very rare in standard writers of the 18th c.," according to OED (1989), and since chiefly in dignified, archaic, or Biblical styles.

unknown.x:
c. 1300, "strange, unfamiliar" (of persons, places), from un- (1) "not" + past participle of know (v.). Compare Old English ungecnawen. A rare verb unknow "fail to recognize; become ignorant of" is attested from late 14c.
In reference to facts, "not discovered or found out," it attested from early 14c. The noun meaning "unknown person" is recorded from 1590s; the unknown "that which is unknown" is from 1650s.

underlying.x: "lying beneath, supporting," 1610s, present-participle adjective from underlie. The figurative sense of "fundamental" is by 1852.

update.x: 1944, in reference to information, 1952 in reference to persons, "supply with the most recent information," from up (adv.) + date (v.1). Related: Updated; updating. The noun is attested from 1967, "new information received; action of receiving new information."

underground.x:
late 14c., "below the surface of the earth," from under + ground (n.).
As an adjective, "being below the surface of the ground," it is attested from c. 1600. The figurative sense of "hidden, secret" is attested from 1630s. In reference to a movement or subculture within a society but separated from or opposed to its forms and norms, by 1953, from adjectival use in reference to World War II resistance movements.
As a noun, "that which is beneath the surface of the ground," 1580s. The sense of "underground railway, subway" is from 1887 (shortened from underground railway, itself attested from 1834).

ugly.x:
mid-13c., uglike "frightful or horrible in appearance," from a Scandinavian source, such as Old Norse uggligr "dreadful, fearful," from uggr "fear, apprehension, dread" (perhaps related to agg "strife, hate") + -ligr "-like" (see -ly (1)). As an adverb by c. 1400.
The meaning softened to "very unpleasant to look at, unsightly, repulsive in appearance" by late 14c. The extended sense of "morally offensive" is attested from c. 1300; that of "threatening painful or dangerous consequences" is from 1650s; that of "ill-tempered, quarrelsome" is from 1680s.
Among words for this concept, ugly is unusual in being formed from a root for "fear, dread." More common is a compound meaning "ill-shaped" (such as Greek dyseides, Latin deformis, Irish dochrud, Sanskrit ku-rupa). Another Germanic group has a root sense of "hate, sorrow" (see loath).
Ugly duckling in the figurative sense of one who grows into beauty or success without promise of it in youth (1877) is from the story by Hans Christian Andersen, translated from Danish to English in 1846. Ugly American "U.S. citizen who behaves offensively abroad" is 1958 as a book title.
Ugsome, for ugly, is a good sample of words which have been dismissed from our language because of their offensiveness to the ear. [Fitzedward Hall, "Modern English," 1873]
Hall notes via footnote that "This and ugsomeness are favourite words with Bishop Latimer" and that "Stubbes has the still more hideous ugglesome."
"ugly person or thing," 1755, from ugly (adj.). The uglies (1846) was slang for "depression; bad temper."

upcoming.x: 1848, "rising;" 1949, "about to happen, forthcoming," from up (adv.) + present-participle adjective from come (v.)). It was a noun from Middle English, "action of ascending" (mid-14c.), also "an attack, onslaught" (c. 1300), and the noun sense of "act or process of coming up" is the only sense in Century Dictionary (1895). A verb upcome, in reference to plants, "spring up, grow," was in Old English.

Utah.x: U.S. territory organized 1850 (admitted as a state 1896), from Spanish yuta, name of the indigenous Uto-Aztecan people of the Great Basin (Modern English Ute), from a local language, perhaps Western Apache (Athabaskan) yudah "high" (in reference to living in the mountains).

Uganda.x: east-central African land, by 1915 in reference to wild game found there, from Swahili u "land, country" + Ganda, indigenous people name, which is of unknown origin. Related: Ugandan.

underwear.x: "undergarments, underclothes in general," 1872, from under + wear (n.). So called because they are worn under one's clothing. "A trade term" (Century Dictionary, 1891).

underwater.x: "beneath the surface of the water," 1620s, from the verbal phrase, which is attested by 1590s as "submerged;" see under + water (n.1). In reference to mortgages in which more is owed than the property is now worth, from 2008.

URL.x: by 1990, initialism (acronym) from uniform resource locator.

upgrade.x: also up-grade, 1847, "upward slope," from up (adj.) + grade (n.). The meaning "upgraded version" is recorded from 1980 (see upgrade (v.)).
"increase to a higher grade or rank," 1904 (transitive); 1950 (intransitive), from up (adv.) + grade (v.). Related: Upgraded; upgrading.

unavailable.x: 1540s, "ineffectual, unavailing," from un- (1) "not" + available. The meaning "not capable of being used" is recorded from 1855. Unavailing has kept the older sense.

utopian.x: also Utopian, 1550s, with reference to More's fictional country; 1610s as "extravagantly ideal, impossibly visionary, imagining ideal perfection," from utopia + -an. As a noun meaning "visionary idealist" it is recorded by 1832 (also in this sense was utopiast, 1845). Utopian socialism is from 1849, originally pejorative, in reference to the Paris uprising of 1848; also a dismissive term in communist jargon, in reference to the ideas of Fourier, St. Simon, and Owen, regarded as "the pre-scientific and infantile stage" of modern, practical socialism.

undo.x: Old English undon "cancel, discharge, abrogate, reverse what has been done, put back in a former condition;" also "unfasten and open" (a window or door), "unfasten by releasing from a fixed position;" also "bring to ruin, destroy," from un- (2) "opposite of" + do (v.). Related: Undone; undoing; undoer.

uranium.x: rare metallic element, 1797, named 1789 in Modern Latin by its discoverer, German chemist and mineralogist Martin Heinrich Klaproth, for the recently found planet Uranus (q.v.).

Uruguay.x: South American republic, named for the river that flows past it, which is from a native name in an extinct language, said to represent uru "bird" + guay "tail," perhaps a reference to some totemic animal. Related: Uruguayan.

USB.x: initialism (acronym) for universal serial bus, by 1994.

Uranus.x:
1800, the first planet found that had not been known in ancient times, it is named for the god of Heaven in Greek mythology, husband of Gaia (the Earth) and by her father of the Titans, etc. Uranus is the Latinized form of Greek Ouranos, name of the god who personifies the heavens, which is literally "heaven, the sky."
The planet was discovered and identified as one in 1781 by Sir William Herschel (it had been observed before but mistaken for a star; in 1690 Flamsteed cataloged it as 34 Tauri); Herschel proposed calling it Georgium Sidus, literally "George's Star," in honour of his patron, King George III of England.
 I cannot but wish to take this opportunity of expressing my sense of gratitude, by giving the name of Georgium Sidus ... to a star which (with respect to us) first began to shine under His auspicious reign. [Sir William Herschel, 1783] 
The planet thus was known in English in 1780s as the Georgian Planet; but that name naturally never caught on "amongst foreigners." French astronomers began calling it Herschel in honor of the discoverer, and German astronomer Johann Bode proposed Uranus as in conformity with other planet names, and English astronomers were preferring Uranus by 1809. However Uranus is said not to have come into common use until c. 1850.
The example had been set by Galileo, who had attempted to name the moons of Jupiter he had discovered Sidera Medicæa in honor of the Medici family, which failed.
 Yet no sovereigns ever deserved better of literature and science than the family of Medici ; and, if their name has not come down associated with the stars discovered by Galileo, so, neither are we to expect, that the name of the most respectable sovereign of the House of Brunswick is to continue united to the discoveries of Herschel. [review of Vince's "Complete System of Astronomy," vol. III, in Edinburgh Review, April 1809]

user.x: "one who makes use of something," c. 1400, agent noun from use (v.). In reference to users of narcotics by 1935, of computers by 1967. User-friendly (1977) is said in some sources to have been coined by software designer Harlan Crowder as early as 1972.

undergraduate.x: "student at a university or college who has not taken his first degree," 1620s, a hybrid from under + graduate (n.). As an adjective, "of or pertaining to an undergraduate," from 1680s. Related: Undergraduateship. British English also used fem. form undergraduette (1920s-30s).

used.x:
"second-hand," 1590s, past-participle adjective from use (v.). Sometimes also in Middle English "populated" (of a city), "travelled" (of a path or way), "experienced" (of persons). The construction in to be used to "be accustomed to, be familiar with or versed in" is by late 14c.
The verbal phrase used to "formerly did or was" (as in the past used to be the present) represents a construction attested from c. 1300 and common from c. 1400. It is from the otherwise archaic intransitive sense in use (v.), "accustom, make accustomed" (someone, to something). The pronunciation is affected by the t- of to. Used-to-be (n.) "one who has outlived his fame" is from 1853. Compare older has-been.

understood.x: c. 1600, "comprehended," past-participle adjective from understand. By 1848 as "implied."

underlay.x: Middle English underleien, from Old English under lecgan "to support (something) by placing something beneath;" see under + lay (v.). Related: Underlaid; underlaying. Compare similarly formed Old High German untarleccan, German unterlegen.

urbane.x:
1530s, "of or relating to cities or towns" (a rare sense now obsolete), from French urbain (14c.) and directly from Latin urbanus "belonging to a city," also "citified, elegant" (see urban). The meaning "civil, courteous, having the manners of townspeople, refined" is from 1620s, from a secondary sense in classical Latin. (Urbanity in this sense is recorded from 1530s.) For sense connection and differentiation of form, compare human/humane; german/germane. Related: Urbanely.
 Urbane; literally city-like, expresses a sort of politeness which is not only sincere and kind, but peculiarly suave and agreeable. [Century Dictionary]

unsubscribe.x: 1570s (implied in unsubscribed), from un- (2) "reverse of" + subscribe (v.). Related: unsubscribing.

United.x: "made into one, put or joined together; allied, harmonious," 1550s, past-participle adjective from unite (v.).

upholstery.x: "upholsterer's work, furniture covered with textile materials, interior fittings made from textiles," 1640s; see upholster + -y (4).

uprising.x: early 13c., "a rising from bed;" mid-13c., "action of rising from death or the grave, resurrection," from up (adv.) + rising (n.). In reference to the appearance of the sun, etc., above the horizon, by c. 1300. General sense of "action of ascending to a higher state" is from late 14c. The sense of "insurrection, popular revolt" is attested by 1580s.

undignified.x: 1680s, of clergy, "not holding a position of dignity," from un- (1) "not" + dignified. The meaning "lacking in dignity of manner" is attested from 1782.

unforgiving.x: "not disposed to overlook offenses," 1713, from un- (1) "not" + present-participle adjective from forgive. Old English had unforgifende. Related: Unforgivingness.

unmanly.x:
late 14c., unmanli, "degrading to a human, savage, barbarous," from un- (1) "not" + manly (adj.). Similar formation in Middle Dutch onmamlijc, German unmännlich.
The meaning "not having the qualities or attributes of a man" (as opposed to a woman or child) is from 1540s.
Old English had unmennisclic (adj.) "inhuman," "un-mannish-like." (adj.). In Middle English unmanful "cruel, unkind" is by c.1500; unmanfully "in a disgraceful manner, dishonorably, sinfully" is by c. 1400. Unmanhede is attested by early 14c. as "discourteous behavior, irreverence, cruelty;" late 14c. as "lack of manly virtue." Both Old English and Middle English had unman (n.) "monster, wicked man, one considered beneath the status of a man."

unblock.x: 1610s, "free from obstruction," from un- (2) "reverse of" + block (v.2). Related: Unblocked; unblocking.

uncircumcised.x: mid-13c., "not circumcised," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of circumcise (v.). By c. 1400 as "spiritually impure, unsanctified." Wycliffe (1382) has uncircumcided. Related: Uncircumcision.

unvarying.x: "not altering, uniform, unchanging," 1680s, from un- (1) "not" + present participle of vary (v.). Related: Unvaryingly. Unvaried is attested from 1560s; unvariable from c, 1400.

underline.x: 1721, "to mark underneath or below with a line," from under + line (v.). Similar formation in Dutch onderlijnen. Related: Underlined; underlining. The noun, "a line drawn below written or printed matter," is attested from 1888.

undemocratic.x:
1832, from un- (1) "not" + democratic (adj.). 
 We repeat, we have no objection that the Democratic Committee should glorify that paper and recommend it to "patronage" (a most undemocratic word, by the way) .... [New York Evening Post, Aug. 12, 1834]

unlatch.x: "open or loosen (a door, etc.) by lifting the latch," 1640s, from un- (2) "reverse, opposite of" + latch (v.).

uncool.x: 1953, in hipster slang, from un- (1) "not" + slang sense of cool (adj.). Uncooled "not made cool" in a physical sense is attested from 1510s.

uncork.x: "draw the cork from" a bottle, etc., 1727, from un- (2) "opposite of" + cork (v.). Related: Uncorked; uncorking.

unseeded.x: 1630s, "not sown," also figurative, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of seed (v.). From 1932 in the sports sense.

unpure.x: "adulterated, mixed; filthy," late 14c., from un- (1) "not" + pure (adj.).

unstack.x: "remove from a stack or stacked position," 1836, from un- (2) "reverse, opposite of" + stack (v.). Related: Unstacked (1772); unstacking.

uppish.x: 1670s, "lavish," from up (adv.) + -ish. The colloquial sense of "conceited, arrogant, proudly self-assertive" is attested from 1734. Related: Uppishly; uppishness.

uncoil.x: 1713 (transitive), "unwind the coils of," from un- (2) "reverse, opposite of" + coil (v.). Intransitive sense is by 1854. Related: Uncoiled; uncoiling.

undaunting.x: 1786, "not quailing" [OED], from un- (1) "not" + present participle of daunt (v.).

uppity.x: 1880 (in "Uncle Remus"), American English, from up + -ity; original context is by Blacks of other Blacks felt to be too self-assertive.

unassailable.x: "not to be attacked or overcome by attack," 1590s, from un- (1) "not" + assailable (see assail (v.)). Related: Unassailably.

unruffled.x: 1650s in figurative sense, "calm, not mentally agitated, not disturbed by violent feeling," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of ruffle (v.). In reference to feathers, leaves, the brow, etc., "not physically disturbed," it is recorded from 1816. Of garments, "not having ruffles," by 1825. A verb unruffle is attested from 1680s.

unceremonious.x: "informally familiar, characterized by lack of ceremony," 1590s, from un- (1) "not" + ceremonious. Related: Unceremoniously.

undercoat.x: also under-coat, 1640s, "coat worn beneath another coat," from under + coat (n.). Extended to coats for housewear or mild weather. In painting and decorating, "a coating to go beneath an outer layer," by 1873. In a similar sense undercolor is attested from 1610s.

uneven.x:
Old English unefen "unequal, unlike, anomalous, irregular," from un- (1) "not" + even (adj.). Similar formation in Old Frisian oniovn, Middle Dutch oneven, Old High German uneban, German uneben, Old Norse ujafn.
Of acts, etc., "inequitable, unfairly distributed," c. 1200; of ground, roads, skin, "not level, rough, broken, rugged," c. 1300; as "unequal in quantity, length, etc.," late 14c., all perhaps formed independently from various senses of even (adj.). Also in Middle English of numbers, "odd" (late 14c.). Related: Unevenly; unevenness.

unvaccinated.x: 1871, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of vaccinate (v.).

unacknowledged.x: "not recognized, not owned or avowed; not noticed as received;" 1580s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of acknowledge (v.).

unwise.x: Old English unwis, of persons, "lacking or deficient in sense, judgement, wisdom, or discretion," from un- (1) "not" + wise (adj.). In reference to actions, plans, etc., "not dictated by wisdom, injudicious," by late 14c. Related: Unwisdom. Similar formation in Middle Dutch onwijs, Old High German unwis, German unweise, Old Norse uviss, Gothic unweis.

utopianism.x: "ideas founded on or relating to ideal social perfectibility," 1783, from utopian + -ism.

unwind.x:
late 13c., unwinden, "undo" (a bandage, cloak, wrapping, etc.), "set free what has been wound," from un- (2) "opposite of" + wind (v.1).
The reflexive sense is recorded from 1740. The figurative sense of "unfold the complexities of" is by mid-15c.; that of "release oneself from tensions, relax" is by 1938. Similar formation in Old English unwindan "unveil, uncover," Dutch ontwinden, Old High German intwindan. Related: Unwound; unwinding.

upturn.x:
1868, "upturned part," from up- + turn (n.). The meaning "improvement" (especially in economics) is from 1930.
As a verb, mid-14c. as "cause to fall or turn from truth; fold back, subvert;" 1560s as "cast or turn over;" 1660s as "direct or cast upward;" from turn (v.). Related: Upturned.

undaunted.x: mid-15c., with reference to horses, "untamed, not broken in," also of persons, "not docile," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of daunt (v.). In reference to persons, the sense of "intrepid not cowed by fear" is recorded by 1580s. Related: Undauntedly; undauntedness.

unlink.x: c. 1600, "separate the links of," from un- (2) "reverse, opposite of" + past participle of link (v.). Related: Unlinked; unlinking.

uproot.x: "remove from fixerd position," hence "remove utterly, eradicate," 1590s (implied in uprooted), in the figurative sense, from the verbal phrase; see up (adv.) + root (v.). The literal sense is recorded by 1690s. Related: Uprooter; uprooting.

umbilicate.x: "shaped like a navel, round and depressed or concave," also "being focal or central," 1690s; see umbilicus. Related: Umbilicate; umbilication.

usurious.x: c. 1600, "practicing usury, taking exorbitant interest for the use of money," from usury + -ous. Earlier was usurary (mid-15c.). Writers in 17c. also used usurous, usurarious. Related: Usuriously; usuriousness.

upcast.x: "turned or directed upward," c. 1400, of the eyes, from up- + past participle of cast (v.). A verb upcast is attested from c. 1300 as "cast or throw up."

undivulged.x: "not revealed or disclosed," c. 1600, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of divulge (v.).

unnerve.x: 1620s, "destroy the strength of, deprive of force," from un- (2) "reverse, opposite of" + verb from nerve (n.). The meaning "deprive of courage" is recorded from 1704. Related: Unnerved; unnerving.

unhorse.x: late 14c., unhorsen, "strike down or throw (someone) from a horse," from un- (2) "opposite of" + verb from horse (n.). Similar formation in Middle Dutch ontorsen.

upchuck.x: "to vomit," 1936, American English slang, from up (adv.) + chuck (v.) "to throw."

uncomplaining.x: "not disposed to complain," 1744, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of complain (v.). Related: Uncomplainingly.

unbrotherly.x: "not fraternal, kind, or affectionate," 1580s, from un- (1) "not" + brotherly.

unconformity.x: "incongruity, inconsistency," c. 1600; see un- (1) "not" + conformity. The geological sense, "condition of not having the same direction or plane of stratification," is from 1829.

ungracious.x: c. 1200, "ungrateful;" early 14c., "lacking God's grace;" late 14c., "unlucky;" senses all obsolete, from un- (1) "not" + gracious (adj.). By early 15c. as "rude, unmannerly;" 1640s as "ungraceful;" and by 1736 as "lacking in courtesy." Related: Ungraciously; ungraciousness.

untolled.x: "not charged a toll or tax," 1590s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of verb from toll (n.).

unevitable.x: "unavoidable," mid-15c., from un- (1) "not" + evitable. Now obsolete; the usual word is inevitable. Related: Unevitably.

unswerving.x: "not deviating from a rule, standard, or course," 1690s, from un- (1) "not" + present participle of swerve (v.).

unchurched.x: 1680s, from un- (1) "not" + churched "committed or belonging to a church" (see church (v.)). A verb, unchurch "expel from a church, remove or exclude (someone) from membership in a church" is recorded by 1610s.

unmistakable.x: also unmistakeable, "that cannot be misunderstood," 1660s, from un- (1) "not" + mistake (v.) + -able. Related: Unmistakably.

unconquerable.x: "incapable of being vanquished or defeated; incapable of being subdued," 1590s; see un- (1) "not" + conquer (v.) + -able.

unendurable.x: "incapable of enduring," 1620s, from un- (1) "not" + endurable. By 1801 as "insufferable, intolerable." Related: Unendurably; unendurability.

unscarred.x: "not scarred" in any sense, 1590s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of scar (v.).

ug.x: early 13c., "to inspire fear or loathing;" mid-14c. "to feel fear or loathing," from Old Norse ugga "to fear, dread" (see ugly). Now provincial, dialectal, or obsolete. Related: Ugging.

uh.x:
inarticulate sound, attested from c. 1600, originally suggesting coughing; suggesting hesitation by 1926.
Uh-huh, spoken affirmative (often ironic or non-committal) is recorded by 1894, metrically imitative ("oh, yes" "It is?"); spoken negative uh-uh is attested from 1924.

Ugaritic.x: 1936, "pertaining to Ugarit," ancient city of northern Syria, and especially to the Semitic language discovered there 1929 by French archaeologist Claude Schaeffer (1898-1982), from Ugarit, which probably is ultimately from Sumerian ugaru "field."

undisguised.x: c. 1500, in reference to things, "not covered with a mask or false appearance," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of disguise (v.). Of persons, attested from 1670s (in reference to Satan).

undiscovered.x: "not yet known, not laid open to view," 1540s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of discover (v.). Related: Undiscoverable.

unclassified.x: 1813, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of classify.

unchain.x: 1580s, from un- (2) "opposite of" + chain (v.) "bind or link with a chain." The figurative sense of "liberate, free from slavery or restraint, let loose," is recorded from 1793. Related: Unchained; unchaining.

unperturbed.x: "not troubled, undisturbed," early 15c., from un- (1) "not" + past participle of perturb (v.).

upscale.x: 1966, "at the higher end of a scale, superior," a commercial word, from up (adv.) + scale (v.3). Verbal noun upscaling is attested by 1945.

unpunished.x: mid-14c., "suffered to pass with impunity, excepted from legal or royal punishment; unavenged," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of punish (v.). Cynical cliche no good deed goes unpunished is attested by 1966.

unidentified.x: "that has not been identified; the identity of which is unknown;" 1812, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of identify (v.).

unaltered.x: "not changed," 1550s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of alter (v.).

urinal.x: c. 1300, "glass vial to receive urine for medical inspection," from Old French urinal (12c.), from Late Latin urinal, from urinalis (adj.) "relating to urine," from Latin urina (see urine). The meaning "chamber pot" is by late 15c.; the modern sense of "public or private fixture for accommodation of men having to urinate" is attested by 1851.

uncritical.x: 1650s, "not able or disposed to criticize," from un- (1) "not" + critical. By 1846 as "not according to rules of just criticism." Similar formation in Dutch onkritisch, German unkritisch, Danish unkritisk. Related: Uncritically.

unglazed.x: 1590s of pottery not given a smooth, shiny surface; c. 1600 of windows not filled with glass, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of glaze (v.).

uncombed.x: "not combed," 1560s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of comb (v.).

unforgiven.x: "not pardoned," early 15c., from un- (1) "not" + past-participle adjective from forgive (v.). Old English had unforgifen.

unload.x:
1520s, in reference to a ship, cart, etc., "take the load from, remove" (as a cargo), from un- (2) + load (v.). The intransitive sense of "go through the process of unloading" is by 1580s.
The figurative sense (in reference to feelings, etc.) is recorded from 1590s; especially as "confide in someone, divulge one's true feelings" by 1885 (to unload one's heart in speaking is by 1720). Used in reference to sales of stocks by 1870, hence U.S. colloquial sense of "dispose of property the holding of which is risky" (1881). Related: Unloaded; unloading.

uncultivated.x: "not cultivated" in any sense: 1640s, figurative, of persons, "not improved by education and training;" 1680s of plants; 1690s, of land, "untilled;" from un- (1) "not" + past participle of cultivate (v.). Related: Uncultivation; uncultivable.

untouchable.x:
1560s, "immaterial, not capable of being touched," from un- (1) "not" + touchable (see touch (v.)). Related: Untouchability.
The meaning "that legally cannot be interfered with" is recorded from 1734. Figuratively, "unrivalled," by 1867. The sense of "too loathsome or defiling to be touched" is recorded from 1873.
The noun, in reference to a hereditary low caste of India, is attested from 1909; the term and the restrictions were made illegal in India in 1947. As an adjective in reference to the caste system also by 1909.

unspecified.x: "not specified" in any sense, 1620s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of specify (v.).

unmatched.x: 1580s, "having no equal, unrivaled," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of match (v.). Related: Unmatchable (1540s).

unsafe.x: 1590s, "involving risk or danger," from un- (1) "not" + safe (adj.). Of places, "dangerous to go," by 1620s. Related: Unsafely; unsafeness; unsafety.

uterine.x: 1610s, "of or pertaining to the womb" (from early 15c. as "having the same birth-mother"), from Old French uterin, from Late Latin uterinus "pertaining to the womb," also "born of the same mother," from Latin uterus "womb" (see uterus).

uncompassionate.x: "unfeeling, having no pity," 1590s, from un- (1) "not" + compassionate (adj.).

unfinished.x: "not completed, not brought to an end," 1550s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of finish (v.).

unannounced.x: 1775, in Ash's dictionary, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of announce (v.).

upland.x:
Middle English uplond, "interior district of a country, hinterland," from Old English upland "the country" (as opposed to the town), from up- + land (n.). As an adverb from mid-13c., "in the country, outside town;" Old English had uppan lande.
From 1560s as "higher ground of a given district." The older sense is now archaic. As an adjective from 14c., "of or pertaining to an inland district," sometimes also "rude, boorish, countrified;" by c. 1600 as "of or pertaining to uplands." Related: Uplandish (Old English uplendisc "rural rustic"); uplander. Jock Upaland was a 16c.-17c. term for a rustic.

unsmitten.x: "not struck or harmed," late 14c., from un- (1) "not" + smitten (adj.).

undeniable.x: "indisputable, evidently true," 1540s, from un- (1) "not" + deny + -able. In 19c. often with a colloquial sense of "undeniably good." Related: Undeniably. Undenied "unchallenged" is recorded from mid-15c.

underhand.x:
c. 1300, under-honde, "in one's possession, care, or power," from Old English under hand "in subjection, in (one's) control or power," from under + hand (n.).
The sense of "by secret means, stealthily, in a surreptitious manner," is attested from mid-14c. Perhaps the notion in the "stealth" senses is of the hand turned over (thus concealing what it holds). Compare Middle Dutch onderhanden "by degrees, slowly," Dutch onderhandsch "secret, private." Also compare aboveboard.
The adjective is attested from 1540s in a literal sense, 1590s as "clandestine, secret."

upward.x:
also upwards, "in, to, or toward a higher position," Old English upweard, upweardes "up, upward, toward heaven;" see up (adv.) + -ward. Upwards, with adverbial genitive, is Old English upweardes.
As an adjective, "directed to or toward a higher place," from c. 1600 (also in Old English). Similar formation in Middle Low German upwart, Middle Dutch opwaert, Dutch opwaart, Middle High German ufwart.
Adverbial phrase upward of "more than" is from 1610s (with upwards). With ages, sizes, etc., and upward, indicating somewhat over or larger, is from 1560s. The phrase upward mobility is attested by 1942 but was mainly restricted to sociologists' jargon until 1960s.
 Under the heading of class comes the most dramatic material in social science—social strivings, the success story of upward mobility, the tragedy of downward mobility. [from review of "The Social Life of a Modern Community," New Republic, April 6, 1942]

urinalysis.x: "chemical examination of urine," 1889, from urine + analysis.

unipersonal.x: "having but one person" (of God), 1810, from uni- + personal (adj.). Related: Unipersonality.

utile.x: "useful, profitable, beneficial," late 15c. (Caxton), from Old French utile "useful" (13c.), from Latin utilis "useful, beneficial, profitable," from uti "make use of, profit by, take advantage of" (see use (v.)).

unpalatable.x: "not agreeable to the palate," also figurative, 1680s, from un- (1) "not" + palatable (adj.). Related: Unpalatably; unpalatability.

unfairness.x: "state or character of being unfair," in any sense, Old English unfægernes "ugliness, disfigurement;" see unfair + -ness. The meaning "lack of equity, injustice" is from 1713, from un- (1) "not" + fairness in the "even-handedness" sense.

unrighted.x: "not made right" in any sense, 1640s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of right (v.).

underwhelm.x: "leave unimpressed, arouse little or no interest," 1953 (implied in underwhelming), a facetious play on overwhelm, with under. Related: Underwhelmed; underwhelmingly.

unhand.x: c. 1600, "to release from one's grasp, let go, take the hand or hands from," from un- (2) "opposite of" + verb from hand (n.).

ukulele.x: 1896, from Hawaiian 'ukulele, literally "leaping flea," from 'uku "louse, flea" + lele "to fly, jump, leap." Noted earlier in English as the Hawaiian word for "flea." The instrument so called from the rapid motion of the fingers in playing it. It developed from a Portuguese instrument introduced to the islands c. 1879. Earlier ukeke is noted as the name of a native Hawaiian instrument, a wooden strip with two or three strings.

unalterable.x:
"unchangeable, immutable," 1610s, from un- (1) "not" + alterable. Related: Unalterably; unalterability.
 He reach'd a middle height, and at the stars, 
 Which are the brain of heaven, he look'd, and sank. 
 Around the ancient track march'd, rank on rank, 
 The army of unalterable law. 
 [George Meredith, "Lucifer in Starlight"]

unbeliever.x: "one who does not believe" in a particular religion, especially "one who discredits Christian revelation," 1520s, from un- (1) "not" believer. Compare unbelief. Old English had ungelifend in this sense.

unsaid.x: Middle English unseide, "not uttered, unspoken," Old English unsæd, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of say (v.). Similar formation in Middle Dutch ongeseit, German ungesagt, Old Norse usagðr.

ungraceful.x: "inelegant, clumsy," 1660s, from un- (1) "not" + graceful. Related: ungracefully; ungracefulness (1650s).

unredeemed.x: 1540s, "unsaved;" 1550s, "not ransomed;" 1805, "not balanced or alleviated by any good quality;" from un- (1) "not" + past participle of redeem (v.). Of bills, notes, stocks not recalled into the treasury or bank, by 1845. Related: Unredeemably.

unwisely.x: Middle English unwiseli, from Old English unwislice "not wisely, foolishly, rashly, carelessly;" see unwise + -ly (2).

unformed.x: early 14c., "without form, shapeless, not having been molded into regular shape," from un- (1) "not" + past-participle adjective from form (v.).

unamused.x: 1742, "not cheered or entertained," from un- (1) "not" + amused. Unamusing is by 1794; unamusive by 1755; unamusable by 1812.

unmounted.x: 1590s, "not performing regular duties on horseback," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of mount (v.). By 1620s in references to guns not mounted on carriages; by 1888 as "not affixed to a mount or backing for display."

underskirt.x: "skirt worn under others," also "the foundation of a gown," by 1832, from under + skirt (n.).

unspoiled.x:
c. 1500, "not plundered, unmolested by robbers," past-participle adjective from obsolete verb unspoil (c. 1400) "despoil, strip or rob of clothes," from un- (2) here probably emphatic + spoil (v.).
The meaning "not deteriorated" is attested by 1732, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of spoil (v.). Related: Unspoilt.

unstinting.x: c. 1400, "unceasing" (a sense now archaic), from un- (1) "not" + present participle of stint (v.). The meaning "lavish, liberal" is attested by 1834.

unasked.x: c. 1200, "uninvited, unsolicited, without prompting," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of ask (v.). Old English had ungeaxod. As "not made the subject of a request," by mid-15c.

unburden.x: in old use also unburthen, 1530s, "to unload" (transitive), "rid or free from a burden," originally and chiefly figurative, "relieve (the mind, heart, etc.) by disclosing what lies heavy on it," from un- (2) "reverse of" + burden (v.). Similar formation in German entbürden. The reflexive sense is recorded from 1580s. Related: Unburdened; unburdening.

unfathomed.x: "not sounded, not to be sounded," 1620s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of fathom (v.).

unpronounceable.x: "difficult to pronounce, incapable of being pronounced," 1712, from un- (1) "not" + pronounceable (adj.).

undismayed.x: "not disheartened by fear," 1610s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of dismay (v.).

unended.x: mid-13c., "without end, not made to stop, interminable, infinite;" late 14c., "not concluded or complete, not brought to an end;" from un- (1) "not" + past participle of end (v.).

unprompted.x: "not urged or instigated," 1650s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of prompt (v.).

unsound.x:
late 14c., of persons, "diseased, wounded," from un- (1) "not" + sound (adj.). The meaning "morally corrupt" is recorded from c. 1300; that of "not mentally healthy" from 1540s. The sense of "not based on reasoning or fact" is attested from 1590s.
Related: Unsoundly; unsoundness. Similar formation in Middle Low German unsund, Middle Dutch ongesont, German ungesund.

underhanded.x: in reference to a throw, etc., "performed or done with the knuckles turned under," 1807, from under + hand (n.), with -ed perhaps to emphasize distinction from underhand. As "in secret," from 1825; as "with too few people," from 1834, from the "worker" sense of hand (n.). Compare underhand (adv.). Related: Underhandedly; underhandedness.

unblown.x: "not inflated or affected by the wind," 1630s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of blow (v.1). Also, of a trump, etc., "not sounded" (1815).

uncirculated.x: 1749, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of circulate (v.).

understate.x: "represent less strongly than the truth will admit," 1781, from under + state (v.). Related: Understated; understating.

unsearchable.x: late 14c., "incapable of being discovered by search, inscrutable," in reference to the ways of the Lord, from un- (1) "not" + search (v.) + -able.

uncompounded.x: 1580s, "not mixed, simple," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of compound (v.).

undying.x: early 14c., undiing, "immortal, not subject to death;" see un- (1) "not" + present participle of die (v.). The figurative sense, "unceasing," in reference to feelings, etc., is recorded by 1765.

unjoint.x: "dislocate (a bone, joint); disjoint, take apart the joints of," probably from un- (2) + verb from joint (n.). Figuratively, "to disunite," by 1560s.

unfurnished.x: 1540s, "not equipped, unprepared," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of furnish (v.). In reference to houses, apartments, etc., "not provided with furniture," it is recorded from 1580s.

unprovoked.x: "not incited," 1580s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of provoke (v.).

uncomparable.x: late 14c., "incomparable," from un- (1) "not" + comparable. The meaning "unable to be compared (to something else)" is by 1826. Incomparable is more common. Related: Uncomparably.

unfeeling.x:
"devoid of kindly or tender feelings, devoid of sympathy with others," by late 14c. (implied in unfeelingly), from un- (1) "not" + present participle of feel (v.) "react with sympathy or compassion." Related: Unfeelingness. Also as a noun, "loss of sensation" (early 15c.).
Late Old English had unfelende "having no sensation;" Middle English had a verb unfeel "be insensible, fail to feel" (early 14c.) as well as unfeelingness "insensibility, loss of sensation."

unremitted.x: "not pardoned, not forgiven; not temporarily relaxed," 1640s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of remit (v.). Related: Unremittedly.

unseasoned.x: 1580s, "not made palatable by seasoning," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of season (v.). The meaning "not habituated by experience" is recorded from c. 1600. A verb unseason "deprive of relish" was used figuratively by Spenser (1590s).

Uriah.x: masc. proper name, in the Old Testament the name of the Hittite husband of Bathsheba; a word of non-Hebrew (possibly Horite) origin, but explained by folk etymology as Hebrew Uriyyah, literally "flame of the Lord." Uriah Heep, character from Dickens' "David Copperfield" (1850) sometimes is invoked as the type of a hypocritically humble person.

unsolid.x: "not solid" in any sense, 1610s, from un- (1) "not" + solid (adj.).

unfulfilled.x: late 14c., "not accomplished," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of fulfill (v.). Unfillable meant "incapable of being satisfied" and "unsatisfying" in different psalms in the 1382 Wycliffe bible.

unsheathe.x: late 14c., unshethen, "draw (a sword) from a scabbard," from un- (2) "reverse, opposite of" + sheathe (v.). Related: Unsheathed; unsheathing.

unsupported.x: early 15c., "not upheld in a suggested course of action," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of support (v.). As "not physically supported," 1630s.

ungotten.x: mid-15c., "unbegotten;" 1540s, "not acquired;" from un- (1) "not" + gotten in its various senses.

underdressed.x: also under-dressed, "too plainly dressed" for an occasion, entertainment, etc., 1759, from under (adv.) + past participle of dress (v.).

unfailing.x: "never coming to an end, unceasing, everlasting, inexhaustible;" hence "sure, certain, always fulfilling hopes or expectations," late 14c., from un- (1) "not" + present participle of fail (v.). Middle English also had unfailable in the same sense (early 15c.). Related: Unfailingly.

uninhabited.x: "having no inhabitants," 1570s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of inhabit (v.).

unpierced.x: c. 1400, unpersede, "unperforated, not having a hole," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of pierce (v.).

unselfish.x: "not unduly attached to one's interests," 1690s, from un- (1) "not" + selfish (adj.). Similar formation in Danish uselvisk, Swedish osjälfvisk. Related: Unselfishly; unselfishness.

unostentatious.x: "not boastful, not making show or parade," 1747, from un- (1) "not" + ostentatious (adj.). Related: Unostentatiously; unostentatiousness.

unforced.x: "not forced" in any sense, 1590s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of force (v.).

unalloyed.x: "not debased or reduced by foreign admixture," 1670s (figurative); 1760s (literal), from un- (1) "not" + past participle of alloy (v.).

unbalance.x: "throw (a person or thing) out of balance," 1856, from un- (2) "reverse, opposite of" + balance (v.) or else a back-formation from unbalanced (1640s). Related: Unbalancing.

unfathomable.x: 1610s, originally in the figurative sense, of feelings, conditions, etc., "too deep to be comprehended," from un- (1) "not" + fathomable. The literal sense of "too deep to be measured" (of the sea) is attested from 1670s. Related: Unfathomably; unfathomableness.

undersell.x: "sell under or cheaper than," 1620s, from under + sell (v.). Related: Undersold; underselling.

unconformable.x: "not consistent, not agreeable or correspondent" (to something), 1590s, from un- (1) "not" + conformable (adj.). Especially "not conforming to usages of the Church of England" (1610s). Related: Unconformably; unconformability.

unrecorded.x: "not registered, not made part of a record," 1580s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of record (v.).

unmovable.x: late 14c., unmevable, "immovable, incapable of motion, fixed in place; not inclined to shift from a moral position, unyielding;" from un- (1) "not" + movable (adj.). Related: Unmovably; unmovableness; unmovability.

unseen.x: c. 1200, "never before seen, unknown, extraordinary, wonderous;" also "invisible, hidden;" from un- (1) "not" + seen. Similar formation in Old English ungesewen, Middle Dutch ongesien, Dutch ongezien, Old High German ungesëhan, German ungesehen, Old Norse usenn.

unaccustomed.x: 1520s, "not customary, unfamiliar," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of accustom (v.). The meaning "not accustomed or habituated" (to) is attested by 1610s (see accustomed). A verb unaccustom (1570s) seems mostly restricted to dictionaries.

unserious.x: "not serious" in any sense, 1650s, from un- (1) "not" + serious (adj.).

unscientific.x:
"not scientific" in any sense, 1771, from un- (1) "not" + scientific. Related: Unscientifically. Chaucer had unscience (n.) "false knowledge or understanding:"
 Yif that any wyght wene a thing to ben oothir weyes than it is, it nis nat oonly unscience, but it is desceyvable opynioun … fer fro the sothe of science. [translation of Boethius, c. 1380]

unseal.x: late Old English, unselen, "remove or break the seal of;" early 15c., "open (a bag, book) that has been sealed;" from un- (2) "reverse, opposite of" + seal (v.). Similar formation in Middle Dutch ontsegelen, Old High German intsigilan. Related: Unsealed (late 14c. as "not marked with a seal").

unseat.x: 1590s, "throw down from a seat" (especially on horseback), from un- (2) "reverse, opposite of" + seat (v.). The meaning "deprive of rank or office" is attested from 1610s; specifically as "depose from a seat in a representative body" by 1834. Related: Unseated; unseating.

unfaithfulness.x: late 14c., unfeithfulnesse, "unbelief, skepticism, impiety," from unfaithful + -ness or un- (1) "not" + faithfulness. The meaning "lack of good faith or fidelity" is from late 15c.

unpurged.x: c. 1400, unpurgid, "not purged" (of morbid matter or evil humors), "unpurified;" from un- (1) "not" + past participle of purge (v.).

unappreciated.x: "not sufficiently valued, not estimated at the true worth," 1809, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of appreciate (v.).

unaffected.x: 1580s, "not influenced, untouched in mind or feeling," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of affect (v.). The meaning "not adopted or assumed, genuine" is recorded from 1590s; that of "not acted upon or altered (by something)" is attested by 1830. Related: Unaffectedly; unaffectedness.

unarmored.x: 1869, originally and especially of warships, "not fitted with metal defense against projectiles," from un- (1) "not" + armored (see armor (v.)).

unascertained.x: "not reduced to a certainty," 1620s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of ascertain (v.).

uneventful.x: "devoid of notable or exciting events," 1800, from un- (1) "not" + eventful (adj.). Related: Uneventfully.

unctious.x: an obsolete variant of unctuous common c. 1600-1725. Related: Unctiously; unctiousness.

unsoiled.x: c. 1400, "immaculate, undefiled," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of soil (v.).

urination.x: early 15c. (Chauliac), urinacioun, "voiding of urine," from Medieval Latin urinationem (nominative urinatio), noun of action from past-participle stem of urinare (v.), from urina (see urine).

unpracticed.x: also unpractised, 1550s, of persons, "unexpert, not having been taught by practice," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of practice (v.). From 1530s as "not done, untried."

uncouple.x: c. 1300, uncouplen, "unleash hounds for the chase," from un- (2) "opposite of" + couple (v.), from couple (n.) in the old hunting sense of "leash for joining a brace of hounds." As "unfasten from a couple or coupling" by late 14c. Later of railway cars and their couplings (by 1858). Similar formation in Middle Dutch ontcoppelen. Related: Uncoupled (by early 15c. as "not united in marriage"); uncoupling.

undocumented.x: "that has not been documented," 1883, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of document (v.). In U.S. especially "not having appropriate legal documents or license." Undocumented worker for "employed illegal immigrant" is by 1977.

unashamed.x: c. 1500, implied in unashamedness, from un- (1) "not" + ashamed. Related: Unashamedly.

unavailability.x: "character of being unavailable," 1839, from un- (2) "opposite of" + availability, or else from unavailable + -ity.

uncorrected.x: late 14c., "not rid of inaccuracies;" early 15c. "not reproved or chastised;" from un- (1) "not" + past participle of correct (v.).

understory.x: also understorey, in reference to forest vegetation, also under-story, 1902, from under + story (n.).

unorthodox.x: "heretical, heterodox," 1650s, from un- (1) "not" + orthodox (adj.). Related: Unorthodoxly.

uncivil.x: 1550s, "barbarous, not civilized, savage," from un- (1) "not" + civil (adj.). The meaning "impolite, not courteous, rude or ill-mannered" is attested from 1590s. Related: Uncivility.

unnaturalize.x: "make unnatural, deprive of natural feelings or character," 1610s; see unnatural (adj.) + -ize. Related: Unnaturalized; unnaturalizing.

unlucky.x: 1520s, "ill-fated, marked by misfortune, subject to frequent failure," from un- (1) "not" + lucky (adj.). Similar formation in West Frisian unlokkich, Middle Low German unluckich. The sense of "boding ill" is recorded from 1540s; that of "having bad luck" is from 1550s; that of "accompanied by or bringing bad luck" is from 1580s. Related: Unluckily; unluckiness.

unsubdued.x: 1580s, vnsubdewd (Spenser, spelling Spenserly), "not subdued" in any sense, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of subdue (v.).

unpretentious.x: "making no claim to distinction," 1859, from un- (1) "not" + pretentious (adj.). Related: Unpretentiously; unpretentiousness.

uncurl.x: 1580s, intransitive, "lose its curl;" 1590s, transitive, "untwist, cause to straighten out," from un- (2) "reverse, opposite of" + curl (v.). Related: Uncurled; uncurling.

uncurbed.x: "not curbed," in any sense, 1590s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of curb (v.).

uncross.x: "change from a crossed position," 1590s, from un- (1) "not" + cross (v.). Related: Uncrossed; uncrossing.

underwriter.x: 1610s, "subscriber," agent noun from underwrite (v.). The sense of "one who carries on a business of insurance" is by 1620s.

undressed.x: "naked (or nearly so)," 1610s, past-participle adjective from undress (v.). Earlier of the hair, "not trimmed or put in order" (mid-15c.).

undisciplined.x: late 14c., "improperly governed, not brought to regular order; untrained" (in virtue), "not duly exercised or taught," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of discipline (v.). Similar formation in German undisciplinirt, Swedish odisciplinerad. The specific meaning "not subject to military discipline" is attested by 1718. Middle English also had undisciplinous "unregulated" (late 14c.).

unwrought.x: c. 1400, "not done;" early 15c., "uncreated, unmade; in an unformed state;" from un- (1) "not" + wrought.

Urschleim.x: "original protoplasm of life," 1921, from German Urschleim "original mucus," from ur- (see ur-) + Schleim (see slime (n.)).

ungallant.x: "uncourtly to ladies," 1710, from un- (1) "not" + gallant. Related: Ungallantly.

unwelcome.x: "displeasing, not well received," early 14c., from un- (1) "not" + welcome (adj.). Related: Unwelcomed; unwelcoming. Similar formation in Middle Dutch onwillecome, German unwillkommen.

unclean.x: Middle English unclene, from Old English unclæne, "morally or ceremonially impure, defiled, unfit for food," from un- (1) "not" + clean (adj.). The literal sense of "soiled, unwashed, dirty, habitually foul" is recorded from mid-13c.

unclear.x:
c. 1300, unclere, "not easy to understand;" early 15c. "not obvious, open to doubt," from un- (1) "not" + clear (adj.). Similar formation in Middle Dutch onclaer, Dutch onklaar, German unklar, Old Norse uklarr, Danish uklar, Swedish oklar.
Of persons, "uncertain, doubtful," by 1670s. In Middle English also "not free of moral impurity, guilty, sinful."

unmanned.x: "not furnished with a crew," 1540s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of man (v.). Also formerly of wild falcons, etc., "not tamed, not yet familiar with man" (1590s). For "deprived of manly fortitude," see unman (v.).

unwifely.x: "unbefitting to a wife," 1864, from un- (1) "not" + wifely.

unshakable.x: "incapable of being shaken," 1610s; see un- (1) "not" + shake (v.) + -able. Of beliefs, etc., from 1670s.

unspeakable.x: c. 1400, "inexpressible," from un- (1) "not" + speakable (see speak (v.), also speakable). The meaning "indescribably bad or wicked" is recorded from mid-15c. Related: Unspeakably.

undershot.x: in reference to a water-wheel, "moved by water passing under," c. 1600, from under + past participle of shoot (v.).

undisputable.x: 1590s, from un- (1) "not" + disputable. The usual word is indisputable. Related: Undisputably; undisputableness.

unicellular.x: "consisting of a single cell;" 1858, see uni- + cellular.

unmuzzled.x: "loosen from a muzzle, remove a muzzle from," also figurative, "free from restraint;" c. 1600, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of muzzle (v.) or else a past participle of unmuzzle (v.), which also is attested from c. 1600.

undecided.x:
early 15c., "not determined, unsettled," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of decide (v.). As "irresolute, not having made up one's mind," by 1779.
As a noun, "undecided persons," by 1968, short for undecided voter, which was prominent in the 1936 U.S. presidential campaign and thereafter. A verb undecide, "reverse a decision concerning," is attested from c. 1600 but is obsolete. Related: Undecidedly; undecidable.

unearned.x: c. 1200, unerned, "not merited, undeserved," of rewards, punishments; from un- (1) "not" + past participle of earn (v.). By 1660s as "not worked for, not merited by labor." Unearned income , from rents, investments, etc., is by 1804.

untraveled.x: also untravelled, 1580s, of persons, "not having gained experience by travel;" 1660s, of roads and ways, "not trodden by passengers, unfrequented;" from un- (1) "not" + past participle of travel (v.).

unambiguous.x: "not of doubtful meaning; plain, clear, certain," 1630s, from un- (1) "not" + ambiguous. Related: Unambiguously; unambiguousness.

uninspired.x: "not inspired" in any sense, 1680s, from un- (1) "not" + inspired.

undefinable.x: "indefinable, not definable in any sense," 1690s, from un- (1) "not" + definable (see define). Related: Undefinably; undefinability.

uplift.x: c. 1300, upliften, "lift to a higher or more erect position," from up (adv.) + lift (v.). By mid-14c. as "raise in rank, honor, estate;" late 14c. as "lift spiritually, elevate." Compare uplift (n.). Related: Uplifted; uplifting.

1845, "act or fact of being raised or elevated," from the verb or from up (adj.) + lift (n.). The verbal noun uplifting is attested from mid-15c. as "action of elevating (someone)." Uplift is attested from 1853 in geology as "an elevation of land." Figurative use in reference to an elevating effect, a mental or moral raising is by 1873.

umpteen.x: indefinite number, "many, a lot of," by 1907, popularized in World War I army slang, from umpty + -teen. Related: Umpteenth.

undersign.x: "sign (a document) below or beneath," 1570s, from under + sign (v.). Related: Undersigned; undersigning. The undersigned in reference to those signing any document is by 1640s.

ungrammatical.x: "not in accordance with the rules of grammar," 1650s, from un- (1) "not" + grammatical. Related: Ungrammatically.

unbreakable.x: "not to be broken" in any sense (earliest reference is to the law), late 15c.; see un- (1) "not" + breakable.

underside.x: "lower surface or side," 1680s, from under (adj.) + side (n.). Similar formation in Dutch onderzijde, Danish underside, German unterseite.

upend.x: also up-end, "set on end, turn end-up," 1823, from up + end. Related: Upended; upending.

uplink.x: communication link from the Earth to a satellite, etc., by 1968, from up- + link (n.).

unrivalled.x: also unrivaled, 1590s, "having no rival or competitor," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of rival (v.).

upwind.x: also up-wind, "contrary to the wind," 1838, from up- + wind (n.1). Originally a nautical term. As an adjective from 1892.

unassigned.x: "not designated or allocated," early 14c., from un- (1) "not" + past participle of assign (v.).

unlivable.x: also unliveable, 1834, "incapable of being lived in," from un- (1) "not" + livable. It is attested in 1869 as "that cannot be lived;" a verb unlive "reverse or annul (a life experience)" is attested from 1610s.

unflappable.x:
"unruffled and calm in crisis or danger," 1957, from un- (1) "not" + flap (v.) + -able. Originally used in reference to Harold Macmillan, British P.M. 1957-63. Related: Unflappability.
 Lord Hailsham, chairman of the Conservative party and lord president of the Council, said at a meeting in London last night that he knew President Eisenhower and Mr Dulles valued the counsel and opinion of a man of Mr Macmillan's integrity, courage, wisdom, and common sense—a statesman of international stature, loyal to colleagues and subordinates, "unflappable and utterly courageous in the face of threats and bluster." [Manchester Guardian, Nov. 1, 1957]

unconverted.x: "not changed in opinion; not brought to accept a (specific) religious faith; not having abandoned sinful life;" 1640s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of convert (v.). Related: Unconvertible.

uncap.x: "remove a cap" in any sense, 1560s, from un- (2) "reverse, opposite of" + cap (v.). Originally of a hat, later of firearms or cartridges. Related: Uncapped; uncapping.

unrefined.x: 1590s, "not refined in manners or speech," from un- (1) "not" + refined. The meaning "not purified, not free from gross matter" is recorded from c. 1600.

unrelated.x: 1660s, "not akin," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of relate (v.). The meaning "not in any relationship" is attested from 1660s; that of "not told" is from 1764.

uncooperative.x: also uncoöperative, 1847, from un- + cooperative (adj.). Related: Uncooperatively.

unbelief.x: mid-12c., unbileve, unbilefe, "absence or lack of religious belief; disbelief of the truth of the Gospel," from un- (1) "not" or un- (2) "opposite of" + belief. Old English had ungeleafa in this sense. As "incredulity" generally, by 1640s.

unopened.x: "not opened" in any sense, c. 1600, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of open (v.).

unshod.x: "without shoes, not wearing shoes," early 14c., from un- (1) "not" + past participle of shoe (v.). Old English had a verb unscogan, unscogian "to unshoe," past participle unscod. Middle English unshōn "remove one's shoes" is attested from early 15c.

untouched.x:
late 14c., "not having been physically contacted, not handled with the hands," also "virginal, sexually pure;" from un- (1) "not" + past participle of touch (v.).
The meaning "left intact, unharmed, uninjured" is from c. 1400; that of "not reached, unattained" from mid-15c.; that of "not used at all" by 1530s. The sense of "unmoved emotionally, not affected mentally" is from 1610s.

urbanization.x: also urbanisation, "process of making urban in character," 1888, noun of action from urbanize.

uptight.x: "tense," 1934, slang, from up- + tight (adj.). The meaning "straight-laced" is recorded by 1969. It was used in a sense of "excellent" in jazz slang by 1962.

unmerited.x:
"not deserved, obtained without service or the equivalent," 1640s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of merit (v.).
 "An ingenuous mind feels in unmerited praise the bitterest reproof. If you reject it you are unhappy, if you accept it you are undone." [Walter Savage Landor, "Imaginary Conversations"]

unbox.x: "take out of a box," 1610s, from un- (2) "opposite of" + box (v.1) "put into a box." Related: Unboxed; unboxing.

unfrequented.x: "seldom resorted to," 1580s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of frequent (v.). A verb unfrequent "cease to frequent" is recorded from 1590s.

unbalanced.x: 1640s, "not poised or in equilibrium," of the mind, judgment, etc., from un- (1) "not" + past participle of balance (v.). In reference to material things by 1732. Of accounts, "not brought into equity of debt and credit," by 1832.

unconventionality.x: "freedom from rules and precedents; an unconventional act or state," 1849, with reference to Shelley, from unconventional + -ity.

uninhabitable.x: mid-15c., "not suitable for human habitation," from un- (1) "not" + inhabitable. Earlier was unhabitable (late 14c.).

undefeated.x: 1701, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of defeat (v.). In reference to participants in sports and games, by 1875.

unabashed.x: "not confused with shame or through modesty," 1570s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of abash (v.). Related: Unabashedly.

upholster.x: 1853, "do upholstery work; furnish with carpets, hangings, etc.," a back-formation from upholsterer. By 1873 specifically as "provide with textile coverings," also generally. Related: Upholstered; upholstering.

undercarriage.x: 1794, "part of a carriage or wagon below the body," from under + carriage (n.). The meaning "landing gear of an aircraft" is recorded from 1911.

unigeniture.x: 1650s, in theology, "fact of being the only-begotten Son;" by 1887 as "fact of being an only child; practice of having only one child;" with -ure + Latin unigenitus, from uni- "one" (see uni-) + genitus, past participle of gignere "to beget" (from PIE root *gene- "give birth, beget").

Ulster.x: northernmost of the four provinces of Ireland, 14c., from Anglo-French Ulvestre (early 13c.), Anglo-Latin Ulvestera (c. 1200), corresponding to Old Norse Ulfastir, probably from Irish Ulaidh "men of Ulster" + suffix also found in Leinster, Munster, and perhaps representing Irish tir "land."

unabated.x: "not lessened, lowered, or diminished," 1610s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of abate (v.).

unbar.x: "remover a bar or bars from; unbolt" a door, gate, etc., late 14c., unbarren, from un- (2) "reverse, opposite of" + bar (v.). Related: Unbarred; unbarring.

unsounded.x:
1520s, "not uttered or pronounced," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of sound (v.1). The word of the same form meaning "unfathomed" is attested 1590s, from sound (v.2).
Middle English also had a verb unsound "make unsound, tear (a garment)," and thus an adjective unsounded meaning "unhealed," also "full of pain or emotional distress."

unclasp.x: "loosen the clasp of," c. 15o0, unclaspen, from un- (2) "reverse, opposite of" + clasp (v.). Related: Unclasped; unclasping.

unsanitary.x: 1854, "not designed or fitted to secure health," from un- (1) "not" + sanitary (adj.).

unfact.x: 1871, "untruth, non-fact," from un- (1) "not" + fact (n.). It is attested by 1954 as "fact officially denied or disregarded," probably a fresh coinage then by the "London Economist," in reference to an edition that year of the Great Soviet Encyclopedia that attempted to scrub the laudatory biography of Beria.

unobtainable.x: 1725, from un- (1) "not" + obtainable (adj.). Related: Unobtainably; unobtainability.

unapt.x: late 14c., "not ready or inclined;" early 15c., "unfit, inappropriate," from un- (1) "not" + apt (adj.). Related: Unaptly; unaptness.

unclothe.x: c. 1300, uncloþen, reflexive, "remove one's clothing, undress, disrobe," from un- (2) "opposite of" + clothe (v.). The transitive sense of "strip (someone) of clothes" is attested from late 14c. Related: Unclothed; unclothing.

underfeed.x: "supply too little food," 1650s, from under + feed (v.). Related: Underfed; underfeeding. Middle English had underfeden "partake of food and drink sparingly" (early 15c.).

unconditioned.x: "not subject to conditions," 1630s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of condition (v.).

unguligrade.x: "walking upon hoofs," 1856, from combining form of Latin unguis (see ungual) + ending as in plantigrade. It is attested in French by 1852, which probably was the source of the English word.

unutterable.x: 1580s, "incapable of being uttered," from un- (1) "not" + utterable (see utter (v.)). As a noun, from 1788; unutterables as a euphemism for "trousers" is recorded by 1826 (see inexpressible).

unchecked.x: late 15c., unchekked, "not restrained or hindered (specifically "not to be prevented from receiving a wage"), from un- (1) "not" + past participle of check (v.1). As "not contradicted," 1590s.

unexpurgated.x: "not cleansed or purged" (of what is deemed offensive or erroneous), 1811, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of expurgate (v.).

unwavering.x: "fixed, not fluctuating or unstable," 1560s, from un- (1) "not" + present participle of waver (v.).

unsentimental.x: "not apt to be swayed by sentiment, matter-of-fact," 1752, from un- (1) "not" + sentimental (adj.). Related: Unsentimentally.

unteachable.x: late 15c., of persons, "not capable of being instructed;" 1660s, of knowledge or subjects, "not capable of being imparted;" see un- (1) "not" + teachable.

undue.x:
late 14c., "not yet owing or payable by right," as a debt, etc.; hence "unjustly demanded," also "not appropriate, unseasonable;" from un- (1) "not" + past participle of due (v.). Formed on model of Old French indeu, Latin indebitus. The sense of "erring by excess, inordinate" is by late 14c.
 There is no need for undue alarm. Well, no, that seems likely. See TRUISM. [Fowler, "Dictionary of Modern English Usage," 1926]

unoccupied.x: late 14c., "idle, not engaged in profitable activity," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of occupy (v.). In reference to ground, etc., "not possessed, not made use of," also of a house, from mid-15c. Of a seat in Parliament, early 15c. By 1940 in reference to the part of France not under German military occupation.

unshorn.x: "not cut off;" of the head, "unshaven;" Old English unscoren; see un- (1) "not" + shorn (adj.).

unoriginal.x: 1660s, "uncreated, without an origin," from un- (1) "not" + original (adj.). The meaning "derivative, second-hand" is recorded from 1774. Related: Unoriginality.

unassimilated.x: "not made to resemble, not brought into a relation of similarity," 1748, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of assimilate (v.).

untrue.x:
Middle English untreue, of persons, "inconstant to friends, kin, one's duty; disloyal; unfaithful in love;" from Old English untreowe "faithless, unfaithful;" see un- (1) "not" + true (adj.).
Of a statement, "false, contrary to facts, erroneous," from late 14c. Similar formation in Middle Dutch ongetrouwe, Middle Low German ungetruwe, Old High German ungitriuwi, Old Norse utryggr.

undertone.x: 1762, "low or subdued tone," from under + tone (n.). The figurative sense of "undercurrent of feelings, etc." is attested from 1861. Of colors or pigments by 1891. Related: Undertoned.

uncollectible.x: 1819, from un- (1) "not" + collectible. Form uncollectable is attested by 1796.

unfeminine.x: 1757, from un- (1) "not" + feminine (adj.). A verb unfeminize is recorded from 1886.

unobjectionable.x: "incapable of being condemned as faulty, false, or improper," 1763, from un- (1) "not" + objectionable (adj.).

unenviable.x: "not to be envied," 1640s, from un- (1) "not" + enviable (adj.). Related: Unenviably.

unadvised.x: late 14c., "not prudent or discrete; ill-considered;" from un- (1) + past participle of advise (v.). By 1851 as "not having received advice." Related: Unadvisedly.

undergird.x: "gird round the bottom," early 15c., undergirden, "gather up from below with a girdle or belt," from under + gird (v.). Related: Undergirded; undergirding.

unethical.x: by 1844, from un- (1) "not" + ethical (adj.). Related: Unethically.

unremunerated.x: "unpaid," 1751, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of remunerate (v.).

unrelieved.x: "monotonous, unvarying," 1764, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of relieve (v.). Earlier "not being given relief, without aid" (1590s). Related: Unrelievedly.

unthinkable.x: early 15c., "too large to be conceived, unimaginable;" mid-15c., "that cannot be made an object of thought, incapable of being framed by thought;" from un- (1) "not" + think (v.) + -able. Related: Unthinkability.

unchristian.x: 1550s, "not professing Christianity" (of persons), from un- (1) "not" + Christian (adj.). Of actions, "at variance with Christian principles, opposed to the spirit of Christianity," from 1580s. Earlier was unchristen "unbelieving, heathen, unbaptized" (late 14c.).

unbeclouded.x: "not covered with clouds," 1709, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of becloud (v.).

unconfirmed.x: 1560s, "not having received the rite of confirmation," from un- (1) "not" + confirmed. The meaning "not supported by further evidence, not firmly established by additional testimony" is attested from 1670s.

undeserving.x: "not deserving, not having merit," 1540s, from un- (1) "not" + present participle of deserve (v.). Compare undeserved.

upside-down.x: "inverted, with the upper part hindermost; into an opposite state of what is normal; into a state of disorder;" late 15c., earlier upsadoun (late 14c.), up so down (early 14c.); see upside (n.) + down (adv.). The so here perhaps meaning "as if." Also up-to-down (c. 1300), up-the-down (late 13c.). As an adjective by 1866.

Ustashi.x: Croatian separatist movement in what was then Yugoslavia, 1932, from Croatian Ustaše, plural of Ustaša "insurgent, rebel."

underling.x: "one subject or subordinate to another, one lower in status or rank than another," late Old English, "one who owes allegiance to a sovereign or ruler," from under + diminutive suffix -ling. Middle English had also overling "a superior, one who is superior in a hierarchy" (mid-14c.).

unawares.x: 1530s, "without being aware; suddenly, without warning," from un- (1) "not" + aware + adverbial genitive -s. The meaning "without being noticed" is recorded from 1660s. The form unaware for the adverb is recorded from 1590s.

ubeity.x: "whereness, state of being in a definite place," 1670s, from Modern Latin ubietas, from Latin ubi "where" (see ubi). Related: Ubication "condition or fact of being everywhere" (1640s).

undoing.x:
miud-14c., "action of releasing (someone) from bonds;" late 14c., "a disbanding or breaking up; action of bringing harm or ruin on (someone)," hence "defeat, downfall, spiritual ruin;" verbal noun from undo (v.).
It is attested by c. 1400 as "action of unfastening bolts or clasps;" from 1530s as "the reversal of what has been done."

Uhuru.x: by 1961 in reference to post-colonial independence of an African nation, originally Kenya, Swahili, literally "freedom."

umbe.x: "around, about; concerning," also as an adjective, from Old English ymb "round," from Proto-Germanic *umbi (source also of Old Saxon umbi, Old Frisian um, Old High German umbi, German um), from PIE root *ambhi- "around," which also is the source of Latin ambi- and Greek amphi-.

unbehovely.x: late 14c., unbihoveli, "unsuitable, not fitting, unseemly," from un- (1) "not" + behovely (see behoove (v.)).

Ursa.x: in constellation names, Old English, from Latin ursa "she-bear" (see ursine). Sometimes alone meaning "Ursa Major."

unallied.x: "having no alliance or relation," 1660s, from un- (1) + allied (adj.).

untreatable.x: late 14c., untretable, "unmanageable, intractable" (a sense now obsolete), from un- (1) "not" + treatable (see treat (v.)). In reference to diseases, conditions, etc., "not admitting of medical treatment," by 1865. Related: Untreated (mid-15c.).

unkingly.x: "not befitting a king, discourteous," early 15c., from un- (1) "not" + king (n.) + -ly (1).

unrested.x: "not refreshed by rest," 1775, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of rest (v.).

underpants.x: by 1871, from under + pants. It took the place of drawers, knickers in this sense in U.S.

unsober.x: c. 1400, "intemperate, given to sudden outbursts," from un- (1) "not" + temperate (adj.). By 1610s as "addicted to drink."

understudy.x: also under-study, 1852, in the theatrical sense of "memorize a particular part so as to be capable of performing on short notice it in the absence of the one to which it is assigned," from under + study (v.). The noun, "one who has understudied a part," is attested from 1848, translating Italian supplimento.

unexcusable.x: late 14c., "unworthy of pardon," from un- (1) "not" + excusable. The usual word is inexcusable. Related: Unexcusably.

unpresentable.x: "unfit to be introduced to company or society," 1828, from un- (1) "not" + presentable (adj.). Related: Unpresentably; unpresentableness.

unheeded.x: "disregarded; unnoticed," 1610s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of heed (v.). Unheeding "careless, negligent" is attested by 1737; unheedful "rash, inconsiderate" by 1560s; heedless is by 1570s. Milton's unheedy swain echoes Spenser (or "E.K.") and Shakespeare.

unfriendly.x: early 15c., "not characteristic of friends, hostile, inimical," from un- (1) "not" + friendly. Similar formation in Middle Dutch onvriendelijc, Middle High German unvriuntlich, German unfreundlich. Old English had unferondlice "unkindly; in an unkind manner." Related: Unfriendliness.

unbefriended.x: "deprived of friendly support," by 1889, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of befriend (v.).

underworld.x:
c. 1600, "the world below this world, Hades, the abode of departed souls," also "the earth, the world below the skies," as distinguished from heaven; see under + world. Similar formation in German unterwelt, Dutch onderwereld, Danish underverden.
The meaning "lower level of society" is attested by 1890; the sense of "criminals and organized crime collectively" is attested from 1900.

unmanageable.x: "not freely submitting to handling, not easily governed or directed," 1630s, from un- (1) "not" + manageable (adj.). Related: Unmanageably; unmanageableness.

unattended.x: c. 1600, "alone, unaccompanied," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of attend (v.). The meaning "with no one in attendance" is from 1796.

umpire.x:
"an arbitrator, mediator, one who decides when others do not agree," mid-14c., noumper, from Old French nonper "odd number, not even," in reference to a third person to arbitrate between two, from non "not" (see non-) + per "equal," from Latin par "equal" (see par (n.)). Originally legal; the gaming sense is recorded by 1714 (in wrestling).
The initial -n- began to be lost by c. 1400 due to faulty separation of a noumpere, heard as an oumpere; see N. The various surviving copies of the popular "Piers Plowman" (late 14c.) have the word in the same place as "a noumpere," "nounpere," "nounpiere," "vmper," "ompere," "nompeyr."

1590s, "appoint (someone) as an umpire," a sense now obsolete; 1610s, "decide as an umpire, settle a matter in dispute," from umpire (n.). Later especially "enforce the rules of (a game) and decide disputed points." Related: Umpired; umpiring.

ungird.x: Middle English ungirden, "remove a belt or girdle from," in part from Old English ungyrdan, from un- (2) "opposite of" + gird (v.). Similar formation in Middle Dutch ontgorden, Old High German ingurten, German entgürten. Related: Ungirded; ungirding; ungirt.

unintended.x: "not intended" in any sense, 1640s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of intend (v.).

unripe.x: Old English unripe "premature" (in reference to death), from un- (1) "not" + ripe (adj.). The meaning "immature, not fully developed, not ready for harvesting," in reference to plants, fruit, etc., is recorded by mid-13c. Similar formation in Middle Dutch onrijp, Old High German unrifi, German unreif. Related: Unripeness.

untroubled.x: mid-15c., of a conscience, "not disquieted" by care, sorrow, business, etc.; from un- (1) "not" + past participle of trouble (v.). Of water, "not raised in waves or ripples" (1610s).

U-bahn.x: German or Austrian subway system, 1938 (originally in reference to Berlin), from German U-bahn, short for Untergrund-bahn, literally "underground railway." Bahn "path, road" is from Middle High German ban, bane "way, road," literally "strike" (as a swath cut through), according to Watkins from PIE *gwhen- "to strike, kill" (see bane).

ultra-liberal.x: also ultraliberal, "liberal in the extreme," 1824, from ultra- "beyond" + liberal (adj.). Related: Ultraliberalism.

ultra-nationalism.x: also ultranationalism, "nationalism in an extreme or excessive degree," 1845, from ultra- "beyond" + nationalism. Related: Ultranationalist.

under-achiever.x: also underachiever, "one whose performance consistently falls below the level predicted by intelligence tests," 1953, from under + agent noun from achieve (v.). Under-achievement is recorded from 1951.

under-developed.x: also underdeveloped, 1892, in photography, from under + past participle of develop (v.). In reference to countries or regions where economic or social conditions fall short of expectations or standards, by 1949.

under-employed.x: "not used to optimum capacity," 1907, originally in reference to working persons, from under + past participle of employ (v.).

under-employment.x: also underemployment, "insufficient use of resources; situation in which there are fewer job openings than people seeking them;" 1909, from under + employment.

under-linen.x: also underlinen, "underclothes made of linen," by 1814, from under + linen.

underutilize.x: also under-utilize, "use at below the optimum or sufficient level," 1949, from under + utilize. Related: Underutilized; underutilizing; underutilization.

unh-unh.x: sound expressing negation or denial, attested in that spelling from 1951. Compare uh.

up-country.x: "the interior regions" of a country, 1680s, from up- + country (n.). As an adjective, "being among the interior" from 1810; as an adverb, "toward the interior," from 1864.

up-current.x: "rising current of air," 1909, from up- + current (n.).

up-market.x: also upmarket, "designated for or characteristic of the more expensive end of a commercial scale," 1972, from up- + market (n.).

up-river.x: also upriver, "toward the upper end of a river," 1773, from up + river. As an adverb from 1848.

USA.x: also U.S.A., abbreviation of United States of America, in use by 1814 in addresses, etc.; not common otherwise before c. 1920. Before then it often meant United States Army. Extended colloquial form US of A is by 1973.

UFO.x: 1953 as an abbreviation of Unidentified Flying Object, which is attested from 1950 in the popular "flying saucer" sense.

UHF.x: 1937, abbreviation of ultra-high frequency (1932) in reference to radio frequencies in the range of 300 to 3,000 megahertz.

Ute.x: indigenous people of the Great Basin of North America, 1826, a shortening of Utah, from Spanish yuta, name of the people, from a local language, perhaps Western Apache (Athabaskan) yudah "high" (in reference to living in the mountains). With combining form Uto-.

Uzi.x: 1959, trademark name for Israeli-made submachine gun, developed by Usiel Gal (1923–2002).

ugh.x: 1765, imitative of the sound of a cough; as an interjection of disgust or aversion, recorded from 1822. The form ough is attested from 1560s.

ump.x: short for umpire (n.), by 1915, American English.

un-.x:
prefix of negation, Old English un-, from Proto-Germanic *un- (source also of Old Saxon, Old Frisian, Old High German, German un-, Gothic un-, Dutch on-), from PIE *n- (source of Sanskrit a-, an- "not," Greek a-, an-, Old Irish an-, Latin in-), combining form of PIE root *ne- "not."
The most prolific of English prefixes, freely and widely used in Old English, where it forms more than 1,000 compounds. It disputes with Latin-derived cognate in- (1) the right to form the negation of certain words (indigestable/undigestable, etc.), and though both might be deployed in cooperation to indicate shades of meaning (unfamous/infamous), typically they are not.
Often euphemistic (untruth for "a lie") or emphatic, if there is a sense already of divestment or releasing: unpeel " to peel;" unpick "pick (a lock) with burglars' tools;" unloose for "to loosen."
It also makes words from phrases, such as uncalled-for, c. 1600; undreamed-of, 1630s. Fuller (1661) has unbooklearned. A mid-15c. description of a legal will has unawaydoable; Ben Jonson has un-in-one-breath-utterable. The word uncome-at-able is attested by 1690s in Congreve, frowned at by Samuel Johnson in the 18th century and by Fowler in the 20th ("The word had doubtless, two or three centuries ago, a jolly daredevil hang-the-grammarians air about it ; that has long evaporated ; it serves no purpose that inaccessible does not ....").
But the practice continued; unlawlearned (Bentham, 1810), unlayholdable (1860); unputdownable, of a book, is by 1947; unpindownable, by 1966. Also compare put-up-able-with (1812). As a prefix in telegraphese, to replace not and save the cost of a word, it is attested by 1936.
With the variety of its possible use, and the need for negatives, the number of un- words that might be made in English is almost endless, and that some are used and some never is owing to the caprice of authors.
Dictionary editors noted this since 18c. but also padded the list. John Ash's "New and Complete Dictionary of the English Language" (1775) has many pages of one-line un- entries; among a dozen consecutive entries are unhaggled, unhaired, unhalooed, unhaltering (adj.), unhaltering (n.), which sorts of words OED (1989) notes were "obviously manufactured for the purpose" and some turn up in other texts only decades later, if at all. (Ash vindicated.)

prefix of reversal, deprivation, or removal (as in unhand, undo, unbutton), Old English on-, un-, from Proto-Germanic *andi- (source also of Old Saxon ant-, Old Norse and-, Dutch ont-, Old High German ant-, German ent-, Gothic and- "against"), from PIE *anti "facing opposite, near, in front of, before, against" (from PIE root *ant- "front, forehead," with derivatives meaning "in front of, before").
More or less confused with un- (1) through similarity in the notions of "negation" and "reversal;" an adjective such as unlocked might represent "not locked" (un- (1)) or the past tense of unlock (un- (2)).

up-.x:
a prefix bringing various senses of up, including "toward a more elevated position; at or to a source, head, or center; in or to an erect position;" originally from Old English up (adv.). It corresponds to Dutch op-, German auf-, Old Norse upp-.
Modern formations with it include upchuck, update, upfield, upgrade (v.), upload, upswing (n.), upscale, uptight, all from 20c.
The prefix was highly productive in Old and Middle English (and among poets of all eras), forming up-verbs where modern English uses "verb up." Some of these (uplift) survive.
