Many do not: Upbear, upblaze, upblow, upbreak, updress, upgive, uphang, upshut, upsit, upspeak, uptie, upthrow, upwake, etc. The old verbs are not so much archaic as dissolved. In a few cases two forms survive to sustain (sometimes contrary) distinct senses: Hold up and uphold; set up and upset.

ur-.x:
prefix meaning "original, earliest, primitive," used from mid-19c., from German ur- "out of, original," from Proto-Germanic *uz- "out," from PIE *ud- "up, out" (see out (adv.)).
At first only in words borrowed from German (such as ursprache "hypothetical primitive language"); since mid-20c. a living prefix in English. Compare also Urschleim under protoplasm and Urquell under Pilsner.
 This prefix is unique because ambiguous, as noted in the Deutsches Wörterbuch: it refers on the one hand to earliness, as ur- relates to a beginning, an initial or primary phenomenon. On the other hand, it also indicates an intensification which is not exhausted in a temporal — or even causal—interpretation. [Sebastian Meixner, "Urphänomen," 2022, transl. Brian Alkire]

ure.x: "effect, operation, practice," early 15c., from Old French uevre (13c., Modern French oeuvre), from Latin opera (see opera). Also "custom, habit" (mid-15c.). To put in ure was "make use of; bring about;" to be well ured in was to be thoroughly practiced in (mid-15c.).

urn.x: late 14c., urne, "large, rounded earthenware or metal vase used to preserve the ashes of the dead," from Latin urna "a jar, vessel of baked clay, water-jar; vessel for the ashes of the dead" (also used as a ballot box and for drawing lots), probably from earlier *urc-na, akin to urceus "pitcher, jug," and from the same source as Greek hyrkē "earthen vessel." But another theory connects it to Latin urere "to burn" (compare bust (n.1)). Related: Urnal.

Ural.x: mountain range between Europe and Asia (the river is named for the mountains), of uncertain origin. Perhaps from Vogul urala "mountain peak" or from Tatar ural "boundary." Related: Uralian; Uralic; Uralitic.

Urdu.x: official language of Pakistan, 1796, formerly also known as Hindustani, from Urdu urdu "camp," from Turkish ordu (source of horde); short for zaban-i-urdu "language of the camp." Compare Dzongkha, a variant of Tibetan and the official language of Bhutan, literally "the language of the fortress." A form of Hindu heavily leavened with Persian and Arabic. "So named because it grew up since the eleventh century in the camps of the Mohammedan conquerors of India as a means of communication between them and the subject population of central Hindustan." [Century Dictionary]

USSR.x: also U.S.S.R., initialism (acronym) of Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, by 1926. The thing dissolved itself on Dec. 25, 1991.

umma.x: "the Islamic community," founded by Muhammad and bound to one another by religious ties and obligations, 1855, from Arabic 'umma "people, community, nation."

unco.x: "wonderfully, remarkably," early 15c., uncou, also an adjective, "strange, unusual," a colloquial shortening of uncouth (q.v.).

uni-.x: word-forming element of Latin origin meaning "having one only, single," from Latin uni-, before vowels un-, combining form of unus "one" (from PIE root *oi-no- "one, unique"). Not active in Middle English but in many words taken from French and Latin; its use with English forms or words was established 19c.

upas.x: legendary poisonous tree of Java, 1783, via Dutch, from Malay (Austronesian) upas "poison," in pohun upas "poison tree." As the name of an actual tree (Antiaris toxicaria) yielding poisonous sap, from 1814.

urea.x: crystalline compound found in the urine of animals, 1806, Latinized from French urée (1803), from Greek ouron "urine" (see urine).

uric.x: "pertaining to or obtained from urine," 1797, from French urique, from urine (see urine). Uric acid is attested from 1800.

uro-.x: word-forming element meaning "urine," from Greek ouron "urine" (see urine).

Ugric.x: 1854 (Max Müller) in reference to the Finno-Hungarian language group, from Ugri, Russian name for an Asiatic race east of the Urals, + -ic.

Ugro-.x: word-forming element in ethnic and language names, in reference to the division of the Ural-Altaic people including Finns and Magyars, by 1848, from Russian Ugri (see Ugric).

Uzbek.x: 1610s, Uzbeg, member of a Turkish race of mixed origin in central Asia; the name is via Russian. Related: Uzbekistan.

uhlan.x: type of cavalry soldier armed with a lance and scimitar, 1753, from German Uhlan, from Polish ułan "a lancer," from Turkish oghlan "a youth." For sense evolution, compare infantry. First integrated into European armies in Poland and other lands on the Turkish border, originally noted also for oriental dress.

umber.x:
brown earthy pigment, darker and browner than ochre, 1560s, from French ombre (in terre d'ombre), or Italian ombra (in terra di ombra), both from Latin umbra "shade, shadow" (see umbrage) or else from Umbra, fem. of Umber "belonging to Umbria," region in central Italy from which the coloring matter probably first came (compare sienna). Related: Umbery.
Burnt umber, specially prepared and redder in color, is attested by 1640s, distinguished from raw umber.
Earlier umber, ombre was used in Middle English as "shadow, shade," also figurative (c. 1300).

umiak.x: large Eskimo boat carrying 10 or 12 people, c. 1743, from Eskimo umiaq "an open skin boat." Said by 18c.-19c. sources to be a "woman's boat," as opposed to the kayak, which was worked exclusively by men.

umpty.x: 1905, "of an indefinite number," usually a large one, military slang; earlier it was Morse code slang for a dash; the form influenced by association with numerals such as twenty, thirty.

unfit.x: 1540s, "not suitable, not adapted" (in reference to things), from un- (1) "not" + fit (adj.). In reference to persons or human qualities, attested from 1550s. Related: Unfitly; unfitness.
"render unfit, make unsuitable," 1590s, from unfit (adj.), or else from un- (2) "reverse of" + fit (v.). Related: Unfitted; unfitting (early 15c. as an adjective).

unman.x: 1590s, "deprive of the attributes of a human being," from un- (2) + verbal derivative of man (n.). The meaning "deprive of manly courage or fortitude" is attested from c. 1600; that of "to emasculate, deprive of virility" is by 1680s.

unmet.x: c. 1600, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of meet (v.).

unpin.x: c. 1300, unpinnen, "withdraw the pin or bolt" from a door, etc., from un- (2) "reverse of" + pin (v.). By c. 1600 as "remove a pin or pins from" an article of dress. Related: Unpinned; unpinning.

unsay.x: mid-15c., unseien, "retract, deny," from un- (2) "opposite of, reverse" + say (v.). Related: Unsaid; unsayer.

unsee.x: late 14c., "fail to see, be unable to see," from un- (2) "reverse, opposite of" + see (v.). Unseeing (adj.) is attested from 1590s as "blind;" Ruskin (19c.) has it as a noun meaning "false seeing."

unset.x: c. 1400, "unsettled, not arranged or allocated;" from un- (1) "not" + past participle of set (v.). By 1570s as "not planted;" 1560s as "not mounted in a setting."

unsex.x: "deprive of the qualities considered typical of one's gender," c. 1600, from un- (2) "reverse, opposite of" + verb from sex (n.). Usually with reference to a woman made masculine. Related: Unsexed; unsexing.

untie.x: Middle English unteien "untether, unleash, set free, undo (a knot)," from Old English untigan "loosen, unchain;" see un- (2) "opposite of" + tie (v.). Related: Untied; untying.

unwed.x: "unmarried," 1510s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of wed (v.). Unwedded "unmarried; celibate" is attested from c. 1200.

unzip.x: "unfasten the zipper of, open by unfastening a zip," 1939, from un- (2) "opposite of" + zip (v.). Related: Unzipped; unzipping.

up-do.x: in reference to a style of women's hairdressing, by 1938; see up (adj.) + do (n.) as in hairdo. Up (adj.), in reference to hair, "worn tied or pinned to the head," is attested from 1911.

U-turn.x: 1934, from U + turn (n.). So called for the shape of the path the vehicle describes in making it.

Uighur.x: by 1747, a branch of the Turkish race prominent in central Asia 8c.-12c., from East Turkic uighur, from ui "to follow, fit, agree" + adjectival suffix -gur.

Ulrich.x: masc. proper name, German, from Old High German Uodalrich, literally "of a rich home," from uodal "home, nobility" (related to Old English æðele "noble," Old Norse oðal "home").

UNESCO.x: acronym from United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization, which body was created in 1945.

UNICEF.x: by 1948, acronym from United Nations International Children's Emergency Fund, which was created in 1946 (the name was changed 1953 to United Nations Children's Fund but the acronym endured).

Urania.x: in Greek mythology the name of the Muse of astronomy and celestial forces, from Latin Urania, from Greek Ourania, fem. of ouranios, literally "heavenly," from ouranos "heaven, the sky" (see Uranus).

Ursula.x: fem. proper name, from Latin Ursula, diminutive of ursa "she-bear" (see ursine). The Ursuline order of Catholic women was founded as Brescia in 1537 and named for Saint Ursula.

ulema.x: "scholars of Muslim religious law," 1680s, from Arabic 'ulema "learned men, scholars," plural of 'alim "learned," from 'alama "to know."

uglify.x: "make repulsive in appearance, disfigure," 1570s; see ugly + -fy. Related: uglified; uglifying.

uglily.x: "in an ugly way," c. 1300, from ugly (adj.) + -ly (2).

ultimo.x: "in the month preceding the present, in the last month and not the current one or any other," 1610s, common (in abbreviated form ult.) in 18c.-19c. correspondence and newspapers, from Latin ultimo (mense) "of last (month)," ablative masc. singular of ultimus "last" (see ultimate). Earlier it was used in the sense of "on the last day of the month specified" (1580s). Contrasted with proximo "in the next (month)," from Latin proximo (mense).

ultra-.x:
word-forming element of Latin origin meaning "beyond" (ultraviolet, ultrasound), or "extremely, exceedingly" (ultramodern, ultra-religious), from Latin ultra (adv. and prep.) "beyond, on the other side, on the farther side, past, over, across" (from suffixed form of PIE root *al- "beyond").
In use from about 1815 (Byron, Southey, Bentham), from French politics (ultra-royaliste "extreme royalist," etc.); "in very common and steadily increasing use from about 1830" [OED, 1989].

umbles.x: "edible inner parts of a deer or other animal," c. 1400, see humble.

unbend.x:
mid-13c., unbenden, "relax a bow by unstringing it," from un- (2) "reverse, opposite of" + bend (v.). The intransitive sense "become unbent" is attested by 1746.
The figurative meaning "become genial, relax" (1748) has a sense opposite to that of unbending "inflexible, obstinate" (1680s), which does not derive from the bow-stringing image.
 [U]nbending, as participle of 
 to unbend, means throwing off stiffness, but as a compound of 
 un- & 
 bending it means never throwing off stiffness ; contrasts, not usually so diametrical as this, often result from the prefixing of 
 un- at different stages ; e. g. in 'lessons learnt & unlearnt', 
 unlearnt may mean either of two very different things. [Fowler]

unbias.x:
"free from bias, turn from prejudice," 1708, from un- (2) "reverse, opposite of" + bias (v.) or perhaps a back-formation from unbiased.
 The truest service a private man may hope to do his country is, by unbiassing his mind as much as possible. [Swift, "The Sentiments of a Church of England Man with respect to Religion and Government," 1708]

unbind.x:
Middle English unbinden, from Old English unbindan, "free from binding, release from physical restraint," from un- (2) "opposite of, reverse" + bind (v.). Similar formation in Old Frisian unbinda, German entbinden, Dutch ontbinden. Literal and figurative senses both were in Old English.
 Suæ huæt ðu unbindes ofer eorðu bið unbunden in heofnum. [Lindisfarne Gospels, Matthew xvi.19]

unbolt.x: of a door, "unlock by releasing the bolt," late 15c., unbolten, from un- (2) "reverse of" + bolt (v.). Related: Unbolted; unbolting.

unborn.x:
Old English unboren "not yet born, not brought into life, not yet existing," from un- (1) "not" + born (adj.). Similar formation in Old Frisian unbern, Dutch ongeboren, Old High German ungiporan, German ungeboren.
By late 13c. as "stillborn, deprived of birth;" also "not reborn spiritually." As a noun, "unborn children; those yet to be born," by early 14c.

unbred.x: "not properly bred, unimbued with good manners," 1620s, from un- (1) "not" + bred (adj.).

uncage.x: "set free from confinement; let or take out of a cage," 1610s, from un- (2) "opposite of" + cage (v.). Related: Uncaged.

unclog.x: "relieve of obstruction," c. 1600, from un- (2) "reverse, opposite of" + clog (v.). Related: Unclogged; unclogging.

undead.x:
c. 1400, undede, "still living, not slain," from un- (1) "not" + dead (adj.). As a noun, in reference to vampires and such as are clinically dead but not yet at rest, by 1897, hence as an adjective, "neither dead nor alive."
Old English undeadlic (adv.) meant "immortal, for all eternity" (compare undying). Middle English undied meant "changed by reversing the process of dyeing" (early 15c.).

undern.x:
Old English and Middle English word for "mid-morning;" in Old English originally "third hour of the day," or 9 a.m. (corresponding to tierce), a word of uncertain origin.
Hence underngeweorc, undernmete "breakfast." Common Germanic: Old Frisian unden, Old Saxon undorn, Middle Dutch onderen, Old High German untarn, Old Norse undorn.
By extension, "period from 9 a.m. to noon;" but by mid-13c. shifting to "midday, noon" (as in undern-mete "lunch," 14c.); and by c. 1400 as "late afternoon or early evening." Compare dinner.

undies.x: 1906, diminutive euphemistic abbreviation for women's underwear (or undergarments).

undone.x: "destroyed, brought to ruin," mid-14c., past-participle adjective from undo (v.).

unduly.x: late 14c., undueli, "without due moderation; improperly, unsuitably;" see undue + -ly (2). From early 15c. as "unjustly, wrongfully."

unease.x: early 14c., unese, "bodily discomfort" (obsolete or archaic); late 14c., "mental or emotional distress," from un- (1) "not" + ease (n.).

unfelt.x: "not felt, not perceived," 1580s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of feel (v.).

unfold.x:
Middle English unfolden, from Old English unfealdan, "open or unwrap the folds of, cause to open," also figuratively, "disclose, reveal, explain, lay open to view or contemplation," from un- (2) "opposite of" + fold (v.).
Similar formation in Middle Dutch ontvouden, German entfalten. Intransitive sense of "become opened out, become disclosed" is attested from late 14c. Of wings by mid-15c. Related: Unfolded; unfolding.
"release (sheep) from a pen," mid-15c., from un- (2) "opposite of" + verb from fold (n.1). Related: Unfolded; unfolding.

unfree.x:
c. 1300, "ignoble, base" (senses now obsolete); early 14c., "constrained, restricted, not possessed of personal liberty;" from un- (1) "not" + free (adj.).
Similar formation in Middle Dutch onvri, Old High German unfri, German unfrei, Middle Danish ufri. In later Middle English sometimes "not possessed of the privileges and rights of a guild, corporation, etc."
Middle English also had a verb unfree "restrict in movement, constrain" (c. 1400), also unfreedom "deprivation of liberty, enslavement."

unfurl.x: 1640s, "spread or shake out from a furled state," from un- (2) "opposite of" + furl (v.). Figurative use, "disclose, display," is by 1670s. Related: unfurled, unfurling.

unglue.x: "separate what has been glued," 1540s (Elyot, rendering reglutino), from un- (2) "opposite of" + glue (v.). Figuratively, "free from strong attachments," by 1619. Related: Unglued; ungluing.

ungood.x:
"bad, wicked, not good," Old English ungōd, from un- (1) "not" + good (adj.). Similar formation in German ungut. Archaic after c. 1300, somewhat revived 20c.
 “After all, what justification is there for a word which is simply the opposite of some other word? A word contains its opposite in itself. Take ‘good’, for instance. If you have a word like ‘good’, what need is there for a word like ‘bad’? ‘Ungood’ will do just as well—better, because it’s an exact opposite, which the other is not. ..." ["Nineteen Eighty-Four"]

ungual.x: "pertaining to or shaped like a nail or claw," 1834, from Latin unguis "a claw, nail of the finger or toe;" cognate with Greek onyx, Old English nægel, Old Norse nagl "nail;" see nail (n.).

unholy.x: Middle English unholi, from un- (1) "not" + holy or in part from Old English unhalig, "impious, profane, wicked. Similar formation in Middle Dutch onheilich, Old Norse uheilagr, Danish unhellig, Swedish ohelig. In reference to actions, attested from late 14c. The colloquial sense of "awful, dreadful" is recorded from 1842 (compare ungodly).

unhurt.x: "uninjured, not physically hurt," c. 1200, from un- (1) "not" + hurt (adj.).

unisex.x: "sexually indistinguishable or neutral," 1968, in reference to fashion styles and appearance, from uni- + sex (n.).

uniter.x: 1580s, "one who or that which unites," agent noun from unite (v.).

unjoin.x: mid-14c., unjoinen, "disjoin, split apart, detach from being joined," from un- (2) "opposite of" + join (v.). Related: Unjoined; unjoining.

unjust.x: late 14c., of persons, "sinful; perpetrating injustice, not acting or disposed to act according to law and justice," from un- (1) "not" + just (adj.). In reference to actions, "unlawful, sinful, wrongful, contrary to justice and right," late 14c. Related: Unjustly; unjustness. A noun unjustice "crime, wrongdoing" is attested mid-15c.

unkept.x: c. 1400, "neglected, unwatched" (of a coastline, etc.), from un- (1) "not" + past participle of keep (v.). From late 14c. as "disregarded" (of a law, etc.), by 1842 as "not stored up, preserved, or retained."

unkind.x:
Middle English unkind, from Old English uncynde "unnatural, not in accord with the regular course of nature" (a sense now obsolete); see un- (1) "not" + kind (adj.).
The meaning "lacking in kindness, not sympathetic" is recorded from mid-14c. In Middle English also used of unseasonable weather, unproductive seed, exhausted soil, chills, fevers, incest, and foreigners.

unknit.x: Middle English unknitten, "untie something knotted or tied, smooth out, undo, untangle, detach," from Old English uncnyttan; see un- (2) "reverse" + knit (v.). Related: Unknitted; unknitting.

unlace.x: c. 1300, unlasen, "loosen the laces of" clothing, etc., from un- (2) "opposite of" + lace (v.). Related: Unlaced; unlacing.

unlade.x: "unload, remove the cargo from," Middle English, from Old English onhladen; see un- (2) "reverse, opposite of" + lade (v.). Related: Unladen; unlading.

unmade.x: mid-13c., "not yet made, unfinished, incomplete," also "eternal" (c. 1400), from un- (1) "not" + made. As "undone, ruined," early 15c., probably here a past-participle adjective from unmake.

unmake.x: late 14c., unmaken, "bring down, dethrone;" early 15c., "undo, destroy, reduce to an unmade state," from un- (2) "reverse, opposite of" + make (v.). Similar formation in Middle Dutch ontmaken, German entmachen. Related: Unmaker.

unmask.x: 1580s in figurative sense, "bring to light, lay open what was concealed," c. 1600 in literal sense "strip of a mask or disguise" (transitive and intransitive), from un- (2) "reverse, opposite of" + mask (v.). Related: Unmasked; unmasking.

unmeet.x: Middle English unmete, "extraordinarily large, extreme in intensity," also "immoderate, excessive," from Old English unmæte; see un- (1) "not" + meet (adj.). Similar formation in Old High German unmazi. The meanings "unfitting" and "unsuited" (for some purpose) are from 1520s. Related: Unmeetly; unmeetness.

unmoor.x: late 15c., "free (a ship) from moorings, loose from anchorage," from un- (2) "reverse, opposite of" + moor (v.). Figurative use by 1866. Related: Unmoored; unmooring.

unpack.x: mid-15c., unpakken, "display the contents by unrolling or untying (a bundle)," from un- (2) "reverse, opposite of" + pack (v.). In reference to luggage, etc., by 1791. Similar formation in Dutch ontpakken. Related: Unpacked; unpacking.

unpaid.x: late 14c., in reference to persons, "not having received what is due," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of pay (v.). In reference to debts undischarged, it is attested from late 15c.

unplug.x: "remove a plug from," 1775, from un- (2) "reverse, opposite of" + plug (v.). In reference to electrical insertion devices, by 1876. Related: Unplugged; unplugging.

unread.x: mid-15c., "not read or perused," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of read (v.). By c. 1600 as "untaught, not learned in books."

unreal.x:
c. 1600, "not real, not substantial, having appearance only," from un- (1) "not" + real (adj.). The meaning "impractical, visionary" is by 1660s. The slang sense of "wonderful, great" is first recorded 1965.
 Unreal City, 
 Under the brown fog of a winter dawn, 
 A crowd flowed over London Bridge, so many, 
 I had not thought death had undone so many. 
 [Eliot, from "The Waste Land," 1922]

unrest.x:
mid-14c., "lack of physical ease, discomfort;" late 14c., "disturbance, turmoil;" from un- (1) "not" + rest (n.). Similar formation in West Frisian onrest, Middle Low German unreste, German unrast, Middle Dutch onruste.
Middle English had unrestful "dissatisfied, malcontent; uneasy, anxious; causing distress or unquiet," which apparently was re-coined 19c. as "not affording or promoting rest;" also unresty "causing discomfort, distressing; restless, bold" (late 14c.). A verb unrest "to trouble, disturb," and a past-participle unrestid "uneasy, upset" also are attested.

unroll.x: early 15c., unrollen (transitive), "open something rolled or folded," from un- (2) + roll (v.). The intransitive sense of "become straight or loose from a rolled position" is attested by 1580s. Related: Unrolled; unrolling.

unroof.x: "remove the roof from" a house, etc., 1590s, from un- (2) "opposite of" + roof (v.). Related: Unroofed; unroofing.

unsold.x: "not traded for money, unbought," late 14c., from un- (1) "not" + past participle of sell (v.).

unstop.x: "remove the stopper from, relieve from obstruction," late 14c., unstoppen, from un- (2) "reverse, opposite of" + stop (v.). Related: Unstopped; unstopping.

unsung.x: mid-15c., "not uttered in a song," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of sing (v.). Especially "not celebrated in verse" (1660s). Similar formation in German ungesungen.

unsure.x: c. 1400, unseur, of a place, "not safe against attack," also, of persons, "lacking certainty," from un- (1) "not" + sure (adj.). By early 15c. as "dependent on chance."

unthaw.x: 1590s, "to thaw," from un- (2) "opposite of," here perhaps emphatic, + thaw (v.). Related: Unthawed; unthawing. Unthawed also sometimes is used with a sense "frozen" (1610s.).

untidy.x:
early 13c., untidi, "untimely, unseasonable, unsuitable" (senses now obsolete), from un- (1) "not" + tidy (adj.). The meaning "wretched, mean; poorly cared for; not neat, orderly, or clean" is recorded from mid-14c.
Similar formation in West Frisian ontidich, Middle Dutch ontidich, Dutch ontijdig, Old High German unzitich, German unzeitig, Norwegian utidig "untimely, unseasonable, unfavorable."
"make untidy," 1891, from untidy (adj.). Related: Untidied; untidying.

untold.x: Old English unteald, "not counted or reckoned," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of tell (v.) in its original numerical sense. The meaning "not divulged or related, omitted from an account" is recorded from late 14c. Similar formation in Middle Dutch ongetellet, German ungezahlt, Old Norse utaliðr.

unveil.x: 1590s, in reference to sight, "make clear, free (the eyes) from a veil," from un- (2) "opposite of" + veil (v.). The sense of "display or reveal" (something) is from 1650s. Intransitive sense of "remove a veil" is from 1650s. Related: Unveiled; unveiling.

unwary.x: "not vigilant against danger," by 1570s, possibly late 14c., from un- (1) "not" + wary (adj.). Middle English had unware (Old English unwær) "incautious." Related: Unwarily.

unwell.x: "indisposed, not in good health," mid-15c., "somewhat ill," from un- (1) "not" + well (adj.). Sometimes from mid-19c. a euphemism for "menstruating." Similar formation in North Frisian unwel, German unwohl.

upbeat.x: "with a positive mood," 1947, apparently from on the upbeat "improving, getting better," attested from 1934 and a favorite of Billboard magazine headline-writers in the early 1940s, from the musical noun upbeat (1869), referring to the beat of a bar at which the conductor's baton is in a raised position; from up (adv.) + beat (n.). The "optimistic" sense apparently for no other reason than that it sounds like a happy word (the musical upbeat is no more inherently "positive" than any other beat).

uphill.x: "situated on high ground; heading or going up rising ground," 1610s (Uppehill as a surname is attested from late 12c.), from up + hill (n.). It is attested by 1620s as "presenting difficulties, attended with labor or fatigue." As an adverb from c. 1600. Grose's "Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue" (1785) has "Uphills, false dice that run high."

upkeep.x: "maintenance; cost of maintenance," 1849, from verbal phrase keep up "maintain in good order or condition" (1660s); see up (adv.) + keep (v.).

uprise.x: c. 1300, uprisen, "stand up, get to one's feet; get out of bed; rise from the dead; ascend to a higher level; flourish, prosper;" of a bird, "take flight," from up (adv.) + rise (v.). From late 15c. as "come into existence." As a noun from early 14c., "resurrection." Similar formation in West Frisian oprize, Middle Dutch oprisen, Dutch oprijzen.

upside.x: 1610s, "upper side or surface, upper part," from up (adj.) + side (n.). As an adverb, "on the upper side" it was provincial English. Adverbial phrase upside (someone's) head in reference to a blow to the head is recorded from 1970, African-American vernacular.

upstep.x: "step used in making an ascent," early 13c., from up- + step (n.).

uptake.x:
"capacity for understanding, perceptive power," 1816, from the verbal phrase; see up (adv.) + take (v.). Formerly with at or in, now usually with on. The meaning "pipe leading up from the smoke box of a steam boiler to the chimney" is from 1839, a separate formation.
Compare Middle English verb uptake "to pick or lift up" (c. 1300), past tense uptook, also in Spenser but now obsolete.

uptick.x: also up-tick, "upward trend," 1962, an economist's term, from the verbal phrase, in reference to recording mechanisms; see up (adv.) + tick (v.).

uptown.x: 1802, "to or in the higher or upper portion of a town," from up- + town (n.). As an adjective from 1838. As this usually was the residential section (especially of a port) the word had overtones of "residential quarter" as opposed to "commercial and industrial district." As a noun from 1946, typically meaning "more prosperous area of town."

uracil.x: pyramidine base, by 1890, coined 1885 in German, perhaps from urea + middle element from German Acetsäure "acetic acid" (or possibly acrylic) + chemical suffix -il.

uranic.x: 1819, "of or containing uranium" (in uranic acid, noted as a new discovery the previous year); see uranium + -ic. By 1860 as "celestial, of or pertaining to the heavens," from Latinized form of Greek ouranos "the heavens, sky" (see Uranus).

urano-.x:
word-forming element, used from 17c. in a sense of "heavens, the sky," from Latinized form of Greek ouranos "heaven, the sky" (see Uranus). As in uranoscopy "contemplation of heavenly bodies" (Blount, 1656); uranography "description of fixed stars, their positions, magnitudes, colors, etc.:" uranometry "measurement of stellar distances" (1715); uranology "astronomy, knowledge of the heavens" (1735).
It is attested by 1850 as the combining form of uranium.

uremia.x: also uraemia, "disorder caused by retention in the blood of urea and waste products normally eliminated by the kidneys," 1857, Modern Latin, from Latinized form of Greek ouron "urine" (see urine) + haima "blood" (see -emia) + abstract noun ending -ia. Related: Uremic, uraemic (1849).

usable.x: late 14c., "fit to be put to use," from Old French usable "available, in use" (14c.), from user "employ, make use of" (see use (v.)). Not common before c. 1840, when probably it was re-formed from use (v.) + -able. Related: Usably; usableness.

usance.x: late 14c., usaunce, "established custom or practice, usage," from Medieval Latin usancia, from Latin usus "use, custom" (see use (v.)). Also sometimes "usury" (1560s). It is attested by 1610s as "time allowed by custom for payment of biulls drawn on distant countries."

utero-.x: before vowels uter-, word-forming element of Latin origin, from combining form of Latin uterus (see uterus).

Ulysses.x: Latin name for Odysseus, from Latin Ulysses, Ulixes. Famous for wandering as well as craftiness and ability at deceit. For -d- to -l- alteration, see lachrymose. Related: Ulyssean.

Umayyad.x: also Omayyad, member of a Muslim dynasty which ruled the Caliphate 661-750 C.E. and in 756 C.E. founded an emirate in Spain, 1758, from Arabic, from Umayya, proper name of an ancestor of Muhammad from whom the dynasty claimed descent.

Umbrian.x: c. 1600, noun and adjective, in reference to Umbria, ancient region of central Italy, or its people, or the Italic language they spoke, allied to Oscan.

unaided.x: "not assisted," 1660s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of aid (v.). Especially in reference to vision or the eyes, 1670s.

unbegun.x: Middle English unbigonne, "without beginning or origin, eternal," from Old English unbegunnen; see un- (1) "not" + begun. The sense of "not yet begun, not yet commenced" is attested by 1560s.

unbound.x:
"unfastened, not tied up," past-participle adjective, Middle English onbounde, from Old English unbundenne, past participle of unbindan (see unbind (v.)).
The figurative sense of "unconstrained" is attested by late 14c.; in reference to printed matter, "not provided with a binding," by 1540s.

unbowed.x: late 14c., "not bent," frequently figurative, "not subdued or subjugated," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of bow (v.). Unbowandnes "unwillingness to genuflect, 'unbowingness,' " is recorded from early 14c.

unclose.x: mid-14c., "open (a container), unlock;" late 14c. in reference to a flower, from un- (2) "opposite of" + close (v.). Related: Unclosed; unclosing.

uncover.x: early 14c., from un- (2) "reverse of" + cover (v.). The earliest use is figurative, "reveal, make known;" the literal sense, "remove a cover or covering from," is attested from late 14c. Specifically "divest of a hat, veil, roof, etc., hence the intransitive sense, "remove one's hat or head covering" (1620s). Related: Uncovered; uncovering.

undated.x: "left without indication of date," 1560s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of date (v.1) "assign a date to." Similar formation in German undatirt, Dutch ongedateerd, Swedish odaterad.
"rising and falling in waves, wavy," late 15c., from Latin unda "a wave" (see undulation). Related: Undate (adj.); undation. A Latin adjective for "full of waves" was undabundus.

undress.x: 1590s, "shed one's clothing," from un- (2) "opposite of" + dress (v.). Transitive sense of "strip off (someone's) clothing" is recorded from 1610s. Related: Undressed; undressing.

"state of partial or incomplete dress," 1680s, from undress (v.). The meaning "ordinary dress" (as opposed to full dress or uniform) is from 1748. As an adjective, "pertaining to ordinary attire," by 1777.

unequal.x:
early 15c., unequale, "uneven in surface, not smooth;" 1530s, "unjust, unfair; disproportioned," from un- (1) "not" + equal (adj.). The meaning "not the same in amount, size, quality, etc." is recorded from 1560s (inequal in this sense is from late 14c.).
Of contests, etc., in which the parties are not on equal terms, 1550s. The sense of "inadequate, insufficient" (to some task or occasion) is attested by 1690s. Related: Unequally.

unflesh.x: "strip flesh from" a wound, etc., early 15c., from un- (2) + verb from flesh (n.). However unfleshed (1540s) meant "not yet stimulated by tasting flesh," as a hunting hound, hence "untried, inexperienced," and unfleshi (early 15c.) meant "bony, scrawny."

ungodly.x:
late 14c., ungodli, of persons or actions, "irreligious, impious, not god-fearing, not in accordance with the laws of God," from un- (1) "not" + godly (adj.). The slang or colloquial sense of "extremely annoying" is recorded by 1840 (in ungodly hour; compare unearthly).
Similar formation in Middle Dutch ongodelijc, German ungöttlich, Middle Swedish ogudhlik. Related: Ungodlily; ungodliness.

unhappy.x: c. 1300, unhappi, "causing misfortune or trouble" to oneself or others, from un- (1) "not" + happy. The meaning "unfortunate, unlucky" is recorded from late 14c.; the sense of "miserable, wretched (originally via misfortune or mishap), not cheerful or gay" is by late 14c.

unheard.x:
early 14c., "not detected by sense of hearing," past-participle adjective from unhear "not hear, refuse to hear," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of hear (v.). The meaning "unknown, new" is attested from late 14c. (Old English had ungehered in this sense). Usually with of since 1590s.
Similar formation in Old Norse oheyrðr, Danish uhørt, Middle Dutch ongehoort, Old High German ungehoret.

unhinge.x: 1610s, "take (a door) from its hinges;" also "to disorder" the mind, etc.; from un- (2) "opposite of" + hinge (n.). In general, "displace, unfix by violence, deprive of stability" from 1660s. Hinge as a verb meaning "to attach by a hinge" is recorded from 1758. Related: Unhinged; unhinging; unhingement.

unhitch.x: "disengage from a hitch or fastening," 1620s, from un- (2) "opposite of" + hitch (v.). Related: Unhitched; unhitching.

unhuman.x: 1540s, of actions; 1610s, of persons, "inhumane, cruel, destitute of human qualities," from un- (1) "not" + human (adj.). A meaning "not limited by human qualities; superhuman, above or beyond what is human" is from 1782.

unitard.x: "tight-fitting stretchable one-piece garment worn by gymnasts. dancers, etc.," 1961, from uni- "one" + ending from leotard.

unitary.x: 1847, "characterized by unity or uniformity;" 1865, "of or relating to a unit;" see unit + -ary.

unition.x: "action of uniting, fact of being united," 1510s, from Late Latin unitionem (nominative unitio), noun of action from past-participle stem of Latin unire "to unite, make into one" (see unity).

unitive.x: "conducive to union or unification, having the property or effect of uniting," early 15c., unitif, from Old French unitif, from Late Latin unitivus, from past-participle stem of unire "to unite, make into one" (see unity).

unlearn.x: mid-15c., unlernen, "obliterate from memory, forget the knowledge of," from un- (2) "reverse, opposite of" + learn (v.). It is attested by 1660s as "unteach." Also compare older unlearned.

unleash.x: "free from a leash, let go (in order to pursue or attack)," 1670s, from un- (2) "reverse, opposite of" + leash (v.). Related: Unleashed; unleashing.

unloose.x: late 14c., unlosen, "to set free (from bonds of sin, etc.), to open (something)," from un- (2), probably used here emphatically, + loose (v.). Old English had unliesan "unloose, set free." Related: Unloosed; unloosen; unloosing.

unloved.x:
late 14c., "not loved, not held in affection, with love unrequited," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of love (v.). A verb, unlove "cease to love" (with un- (2)) is attested from late 14c. Old English unlofod meant "unpraised."
 I have told you, reader, that I had learnt to love Mr. Rochester: I could not unlove him now, merely because I found that he had ceased to notice me. ["Jane Eyre," 1847] 
 He that can love unloved again, 
 Hath better store of love than brain 
 [Robert Ayton (1570-1638)] 
Unlovable (also unloveable) is attested from 1560s.

unmeant.x: "not intended, undesigned," 1630s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of mean (v.).

unmoved.x: late 14c., unmeved, "not affected by emotion or excitement," in astronomy, "fixed in position," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of move (v.). The meaning "not transferred from one place to anpother" is by mid-15c.

unnamed.x: mid-15c., "not mentioned by name, unspoken, unsaid," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of name (v.). The meaning "not provided with a name" is from 1610s. Similar formation in Old Frisian unnamed, Middle Dutch ongenaemt. Related: Unnamable.

unowned.x: 1610s, "unpossessed, not claimed as property," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of own (v.). From 1715 as "unacknowledged, unavowed."

unpaved.x: "not covered with paving," 1530s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of pave (v.).

unplace.x: 1510s, "displace" (implied in unplaced), from un- (2) "reverse, opposite of" + place (v.). Related: Unplacing.

unquiet.x: late 14c., of persons, conscience, the tongue, "troublemaking, restless, active, not calm or tranquil," from un- (1) "not" + quiet (adj.). Related: Unquietly; unquietness.

unquote.x: 1912, in telegraph messages, where punctuation had to be spelled out and quote and unquote were used in place of the quotation marks; from un- (2) "reverse, opposite of" + quote (v.). Quote unquote spoken together as a verbal formula to indicate quotation of the word or phrase to follow (often with ironic intent) is attested by 1920.

unrated.x: "not rated" in any sense, 1640s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of rate (v.2).

unready.x:
early 14c., unredi, "not prepared," from un- (1) "not" + ready (adj.). By 1590s as "not quick or prompt." Related: Unreadily; unreadiness.
In English history, as the sobriquet of Anglo-Saxon king Ethelred the Unready, it is a different word, Middle English unredi, equivalent of Old English ungeræd "ill-advised, 'rede-less,' no-counsel." Old English ræd "advice, counsel" is related to read (v.). 
By c. 1200 it was used (Etheldredus Unrad, Eilred Unred) in connection with King Æðelræd II (968-1016), whose ineffectual reign was marked by viking incursions. The original title was Unred "folly, imprudence; bad counsel, foolish or wicked advice" and it plays on the name Ethelred, which means "good-counsel." As Unready, it is attested by 1580s.
Rede "counsel" (q.v.) survived in poetic usage to 17c. and is preserved in other names (Alfred). An attempted revival by Scott (19c.) failed, though Tolkien put it in "Lord of the Rings."

unruled.x: late 14c., "ungoverned, uncontrolled," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of rule (v.). By mid-15c. as "unadjudicated;" by 1888 as "not having ruled lines, not marked with lines by means of a rule," of writing paper, etc.

unsated.x: "not sated" in any sense, 1690s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of sate (v.).

unscrew.x: "draw the screws from, unfasten by taking out the screws," 1650s, from un- (2) "opposite of" + screw (v.). Related: Unscrewed; unscrewing.

unstick.x: "free," as one thing stuck to another, 1706, from un- (2) "reverse, opposite of" + stick (v.). Related: Unstuck; unsticking.

unstuck.x: 1840, "unpierced;" 1860, "unglued," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of stick (v.).

untaken.x: mid-14c., "uncaptured," from un- (1) "not" + taken. From 15c. in other senses of taken.

untamed.x:
mid-14c., figurative, of vices, etc., "not mastered or overcome;" late 14c., of an animal, "undomesticated, unbroken to use by humans," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of tame (v.).
Similar formation in Old English untemed, Old Norse utamdr, Old High German ungizamot. Also untame (adj.), late 14c.; a verb untame is attested from 1640s. Related: Untamable, untameable (1570s).

unteach.x: "cause to forget or disbelieve what has been taught," 1530s, from un- (2) "reverse, opposite of" + teach (v.). Related: Unteaching.

untried.x: 1510s, "not proven or put to a test," from un- (1) "not" + tried. As "not heard or determined by law or a judge," 1610s.

untruth.x: Middle English untreuth, from Old English untreowþ "unfaithfulness, treachery, character of being inconstant to duty, comrades, etc.," from un- (1) "not" + truth (n.). The meaning "falsehood" is attested from mid-15c., as is that of "a lie, a false assertion." Related: Untruthful. Similar formation in Old Norse utrygð.

unweave.x: "pull or draw apart what has been woven," literally or figuratively, 1540s, from un- (2) "reverse, opposite of" + weave (v.1) . Related: Unweaving; unwoven.

unwound.x: "no longer coiled or twisted," 1707, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of wind (v.1).

unwoven.x: "not woven" in any sense, early 15c., from un- (1) "not" + woven.

updraft.x: also updraught, "rising air current," 1909, in reference to aircraft, from up (adj.) + draft (n.). There is an updraught from late 15c., apparently in reference to tidal waters.

upfield.x: "toward the end of the (football) field nearest the goal," 1951, from up- + field (n.).

upraise.x: early 13c., upreisen, "raise to a higher level, lift up; elevate in rank or status; erect (a wall); raise from the dead, restore to life;" from up (adv.) + raise (v.). Related: Upraised; upraising. An upraiser was "one who helps someone up from misfortune," but also an instigator.

upshift.x: 1839, "movement upward," from up (adj.) + shift (n.1). Specifically as "change to a higher gear in a motor vehicle" by 1951.

upskirt.x:
by 1997, from up (adv.) + skirt (n.). As a verb by 2008.
 "Upskirt" videos, usually taken using low-hanging bags, feature up-close-and-personal crotch shots of leggy, panty-clad young women. [Weekly World News, Sept. 29, 1998]

upstage.x: 1855 in theatrical jargon, "to the rear of the stage," from up (adv.) + stage (n.). From 1901 as an adjective, 1916 as a noun. The notion in the verb (1921) is of drawing attention to oneself (and away from a fellow actor) by moving upstage, so that the other actor must face away from the audience. Related: Upstaged; upstaging.

upstart.x: 1550s, "one newly risen from a humble position to one of power, importance, or rank, a parvenu," also start-up, from up (adv.) + start (v.) in the sense of "jump, spring, rise." The image is of one who springs up suddenly (mushroom in the same sense and for the same reason is from 1590s). As an adjective from 1560s. Compare the archaic verb upstart "to spring to one's feet," attested from c. 1300.

upstate.x: "in the part of a state higher than another or more remote from the capital," by 1892, American English, from up- + state (n.). Earliest in accounts of New York politics; also by 1892 as an adjective. Related: Upstater.

upsurge.x: "a rise or increase of feeling, a surging up," by 1916, from up- + surge (n.). By 1935 as "sharp rise in economic activity."

upsweep.x: 1898, "a long, curving, upward movement, a sweeping upward," from up- + sweep (n.). As the name of a hair-style, by 1946; upswept, of hair, is by 1938, and compare up-do.

upswing.x: 1922, in golf, "backswing," from up- + swing (n.). The sense in economics is attested from 1934, "upturn, upsurge, upward movement or trend."

uranian.x:
"homosexual," 1893, from the reference to Aphrodite in Plato's "Symposium;" Urania "Heavenly" (Greek Ourania; see Uranus) being an epithet of Aphrodite as born of Uranus and also as distinguished from the vulgar Venus of commonplace lust.
 But the son of the heavenly Aphrodite is sprung from a mother in whose birth the female has no part, but she is from the male only; this is that love which is of youths only, and the goddess being older has nothing of wantonness. Those who are inspired by this love turn to the male, and delight in him who is the more valiant and intelligent nature; any one may recognize the pure enthusiasts in the very character of their attachments. [Benjamin Jowett, transl., 1874] 
Also as a noun, "a homosexual person" (1908). Related uranism "homosexuality" (1893).

urinary.x: "of or pertaining to urine," 1570s, from Modern Latin urinarius, from Latin urina (see urine). Urinative "causing urination, diuretic" is from early 15c.

urinate.x: "discharge urine, make water, micturate," 1590s, a back-formation from urination or else from Medieval Latin urinatus, past participle of urinare, from urina (see urine). Earlier verb in medicine was simply urine (Chauliac, early 15c.). Related: Urinated; urinating.

urology.x: "urinology, study of the urinary organs," 1753, from uro- + -logy.

usurper.x: early 15c., "one who seizes power or property without right; one who unlawfully assumes royal authority;" agent noun from usurp (v.). Fem. form usurpress is from 1630s; usurpatrix (Cotgrave, 1611) seems a dictionary word.

utterly.x: "completely, entirely, to an absolute degree," late 14c., from utter (adj.)) + -ly (2). In 14c. also "to be sure, precisely, exactly." Earlier the same word meant "truly, plainly, outspokenly," from utter (v.). Old English uterlic (adj.) meant "external," hence early Middle English outreli "outwardly, superficially; unashamedly." Compare German äusserlich.

usurer.x: late 13c., "one who lends money at interest," but later especially, and then exclusively, "one who lends money at a rate of interest considered exorbitant," from Anglo-French usurer, Old French usurier, usureor, from Medieval Latin usurarius "money-lender, usurer," from Latin usurarius (adj.) "pertaining to interest; that pays interest," from usura (see usury).

unarmed.x: c. 1300, "with armor removed," from un- (1) "not" + armed, or else it is a past-participle adjective from unarm "strip of armor" (c. 1300), from un- (2) "opposite of" + arm (v.). The meaning "not fitted to attack, weaponless" is from late 14c.

unbosom.x: "disclose in confidence" (secret opinions or feelings), 1580s, from un- (1) + bosom. Compare embosom and the colloquial get (something) off (one's) chest. Unbreast in the same sense is attested 1550s. Related: Embosomer.

unfazed.x: 1933, American English, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of faze (v.).

unglued.x: 1690s, "having no glue," past participle of unglue (v.). To come unglued in the figurative sense of "fail completely, break down" is recorded from 1922, earlier in reference to furniture.

unslain.x: mid-13c., "not killed, alive," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of slay (v.).

ugliness.x:
"repulsiveness of appearance," also "horror, dread," late 14c., uglinesse, from ugly + -ness.
Middle English also had ugsomeness "dread, horror, fear," also "revulsion, loathing" (early 15c.).

ulcerate.x: early 15c. (Chauliac), ulceraten, "form an ulcer or ulcers, cause festering sores on the body," from Latin ulceratus, past participle of ulcerare, from stem of ulcus "ulcer" (see ulcer). Middle English also had ulceren (c. 1400).

ulcerous.x: "having or characterized by festering sores," early 15c. (Chauliac), from Latin ulcerosus "full of sores," from stem of ulcus (see ulcer).

ultimity.x: "final development or last stage of anything," from Medieval Latin ultimitatem (nominative ultimitas), noun of condition from past-participle stem of ultimare "be final, come to an end" (see ultimate).

unafraid.x: "lacking fear," early 15c., from un- (1) "not" + afraid. Alternative unaffrighted is by 1580s.

unbeaten.x: late 13c., "not subjected to blows, not struck," from un- (1) + beaten. In the sense of "not conquered or surpassed" it is attested by 1757. Old English had ungebeaten "unwrought, unstruck."

unbidden.x: Middle English unbiden, "not asked, commanded, or ordered," from Old English unbedene, "not asked or invited," from un- (1) "not" + bidden. Similar formation in Middle Dutch ongebeden, German ungebeten, Old Norse ubeðinn.

unbroken.x:
c. 1300, "unviolated, not infringed," in reference to vows or compacts, from un- (1) "not" + broken. Old English had ungebrocen.
It is attested from late 15c. in reference to material things, "whole, entire, not fractured;" 1510s in reference to courage, spirit, etc., "not weakened or crushed." It is attested by 1530s in reference to horses not tamed or made tractable; 1570s of ground not plowed, 1560s in reference to the flow of time, "uninterrupted."

unbuckle.x: "release from a fastening by buckles, unfasten or release the clasp of," late 14c., unbokelen, from un- (2) "reverse of" + buckle (v.1). Related: Unbuckled; unbuckling.

unbundle.x: "remove or release from a bundle," c. 1600, from un- (2) "reverse of" + bundle (v.). By 1969 in reference to systems of charging for computer software and equipment. Related: Unbundled; unbundling.

unburied.x: "not interred," Old English unbyrged "unburied," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of bury (v.).

unbutton.x: early 14c., unbotonen, "undo the fastenings of a garment; open (a garment, etc.) by separating the buttons and button-holes," from un- (2) "opposite of" + button (v.). Related: Unbuttoned; unbuttoning.

uncalled.x:
c. 1400, uncallid, of persons, "not summoned," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of call (v.). Similar formation in Swedish okallad, Danish ukaldet.
Especially "not summoned to do something by some power or authority," hence uncalled for "unnecessary, intrusive, not required," attested by 1610s.

uncaring.x: 1786, from un- (1) "not" + caring. Related: Uncaringly. Uncared-for is attested from 1590s.

unchaste.x: late 14c., "sexually impure, lecherous, lascivious," from un- (1) "not" + chaste. Related: Unchastely; unchastity "sexual impurity; unchaste act" (late 14c.).

uncomely.x: c. 1200, uncomli, "improper, unseemly, indecent," from un- (1) "not" + comely. By c. 1400 as "wanting grace, not pleasing to the senses." Related: Uncomeliness.

underage.x: also under-age, "done by one below the legal age to do it," by 1978, from under age "below the legal age of majority," 1590s, from under + age (n.).

underarm.x: 1816, "underhand" (in cricket, in reference to a style of throwing), from under + arm (n.1). Attested from 1908 in dressmaking in reference to "seams on the lower half of the arm-hole;" as a euphemism for armpit, it is attested from 1930s, popularized by advertisers of personal-care products.

underbid.x: 1610s, "make too low an offer," from under + bid (v.). By 1670s as "offer less than another" (at auction, etc.). In bridge by 1908. Related: Underbidding.

underdog.x:
"the beaten dog in a fight," 1887, from under + dog (n.). Compare top dog "dominant person in a situation or hierarchy" (see top (adj.)). Its opposite, overdog, is attested by 1908.
 I'm a poor underdog
 But tonight I will bark
 With the great Overdog
 That romps through the dark.
 [from "Canis Major," Robert Frost, 1928]

underman.x: also under-man, "furnish with an insufficient number of men," 1867, implied in under-manned, from under + man (v.). Related: Undermanning.

underpay.x: "pay insufficiently," 1817, from under + pay (v.). Related: underpaid (1762); underpaying.

underpin.x: "support or prop, place something under (something) for a foundation," 1520s, figurative; 1530s (literal), from under + pin (v.). Related: Underpinned; underpinning.

undersea.x: "situated under the surface of the sea," 1610s, from under + sea.

underset.x: "support by a prop or stay," Old English undersetten; see under + set (v.). Related: Undersetting.

undertow.x: "a current of water below the surface moving in a different direction from the surface current," also "backdraft of a breaking wave on a beach;" 1798, from under + tow (n.2) "act of towing."

underuse.x: also under-use, "make insufficient use of," by 1960, from under + use (v.). Related: Underused; underusing.

unending.x: "endless, having no end," 1660s, from un- (1) "not" + present participle of end (v.). Related: Endlessly; endlessness. Early Middle English had unendelich "infinitely."

unequity.x: late 14c., unequite, "wickedness;" c. 1400, "injustice;" see un- (1) "not" + equity.

unerring.x: "making no mistake, not missing its mark or going astray," 1640s (implied in unerringly), from un- (1) "not" + verbal noun from err.

unfading.x: "not liable to lose freshness or color," also figurative, "not liable to wither or decay," 1650s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of fade (v.). Related: Unfadingly; unfadingness.

unfamous.x: late 14c., "not well known, obscure, lost to fame," from un- (1) "not" + famous (adj.). Also 14c.-16c. as "notably bad," a sense now only in infamous.

unfasten.x: c. 1200, unfastnen, "make less binding" (figurative, in religion), from un- (2) "opposite of" + fasten (v.) and in part from Old English unfæstnian "to unfasten, loosen, unbind." Related: Unfastened; unfastening.

unfenced.x: 1540s, figurative, "defenseless, unguarded," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of fence (v.) in the old sense of "defend." By c. 1600 as "having no fence."

unfetter.x: mid-14c., unfeteren, "free from fetters, unshackle," from un- (2) "opposite of" + fetter (v.). The figurative sense is recorded from late 14c. Related: Unfettered; unfettering.

unfreeze.x: 1580s, "cause to thaw," from un- (2) "opposite of" + freeze (v.). Figuratively, of restrictions on assets, etc., from 1630s. Related: Unfrozen.

unfriend.x:
in the Facebook sense, attested from November 2007, from un- (2) "opposite of" + friend (v.).
Unfriended (adj.) is by 1510s in the sense "friendless." A noun unfriend "enemy, adversary" is recorded from late 13c., survived chiefly in Scottish, and was still in use in 19c. Unfriendship "enmity" is from mid-14c.

unfunded.x: "not funded, floating" (of a debt), 1766, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of fund (v.).

ungentle.x: late 14c., of persons, "not noble or well-bred," from un- (1) "not" + gentle (adj.). By c. 1500 of actions or things, "rough, harsh." Ungenteel "impolite, rude" is from 1630s.

unguided.x: mid-15c., "without a leader, unprotected;" 1580s, "left to take its own way, not led or conducted;" from un- (1) "not" + past participle of guide (v.).

unhappen.x: of an event, "become as though it had never occurred," 1805, from un- (2), denoting reversal, + happen (v.). Related: Unhappened; unhappening.

unharmed.x: "not injured," mid-14c., from un- (1) "not" + past participle of harm (v.).

unhinged.x: "thrown into confusion," 1719, past-participle adjective from unhinge. Specifically of persons or the mind by 1732.

unhoused.x: c. 1600, "not sheltered by a house," especially "driven from a home or shelter," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of house (v.). Of a place, "having no houses," 1580s. Middle English had a verb unhousen (mid-14c.) "turn (someone) out of a house, drive from habitation or shelter."

unicycle.x: type of vehicle with one wheel, a form of velocipede, 1869, American English, from Latin uni- "one" (see uni-) + -cycle, from bicycle (the element is from Greek kyklos "circle, wheel").

uninvite.x: "countermand the invitation of," 1660s, from un- (2) "opposite of" + invite (v.).

unionism.x: 1845, "principle of uniting," from union + -ism. By 1864 in U.S. as "attachment or loyalty to the federal union." By 1869 as short for trade-unionism.

unionize.x: 1841, "make into a union" (transitive), from union + -ize. The meaning "form into a trade union" is from 1887. Intransitive sense by 1969. Related: Unionized; unionizing.

unipolar.x: 1807, originally in electricity, "exhibiting one kind of polarity," from uni- + polar. Related: Unipolarity.

univalve.x: in reference to mollusks and shells consisting of a single piece, 1660s (noun and adjective), from uni- + valve. Contrasted to bivalve.

unkenned.x: "unknown," c. 1300, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of ken (v.) "to know, understand."

unkindly.x: c. 1200, unkindeli, "unsuitably, improperly, in a manner not befitting one's nature or status," from un- (1) "not" + kindly (adv.). By late 13c. especially as "with unnatural disregard for one's parents." From early 14c. as "indecently, in a manner contrary to natural moral law." From mid-15c. as "discourteously, maliciously." Related: Unkindliness.

early 13c., unkindeli, "not natural, unnatural" (sense now obsolete), from un- (1) "not" + kindly (adj.). It is attested from mid-13c. as "contrary to moral law, perverted, indecent;" by c. 1300 as "without natural affection (for a parent), unfraternal." Old English had ungecyndelic. Related: Unkindliness.

unkissed.x:
"having not been kissed," late 14c., unkiste, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of kiss (v.). Often in proverbs. A verb unkiss, "retract or annul by kissing again" (1560s) is rare.
 And also we schulen go vnkist 
  boþe at þe dore & at þe gate ; 
 And for al þe cheer þat we can make, 
  þan is no ioie of oure visage : 
 Whanne oure bewte schal aslake, 
  god send us paciens in oure olde age ! 
 [c. 1450]

unleaded.x: 1610s, "having no lead covering or finishing" (of a roof, etc.), from un- (1) "not" + leaded (see lead (v.2)). In reference to gasoline, from 1965. In reference to printed text, "not spaced with leads," from 1902.

unlimber.x: 1760, in military use, "detach the limbers from, free (a gun) from its limber," usually for the purpose of bringing it into action, from un- (2) "opposite of" + limber "attach a gun to its limber" (see limber (n.)). The figurative sense is attested from 1864. Related: Unlimbered; unlimbering.

unlisted.x: "not placed on a list," 1640s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of list (v.3). In reference to stocks, securities, etc., attested by 1881; of phone numbers by 1904 (American English).

unlooked.x: early 14c., "neglected, not looked after, unattended," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of look (v.). Unlooked for "unexpected, not anticipated" is attested from 1530s.

unlovely.x: late 14c., "not evoking feelings of love, disagreeable;" also "physically unattractive, ugly;" from un- (1) "not" + lovely. Related: Unloveliness. Middle English also had unlofsum ("unlovesome") "ugly, hideous, undesirable."

unmaking.x: "ruin, destruction; act or process of destroying; that which ruins or unmakes;" 1590s, verbal noun from unmake (v.).

unmarked.x: c. 1400, "having been given no mark," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of mark (v.). Similar formation in Old Norse umarkaðr. The meaning "not noticed or observed" is recorded from 1530s.

unmarred.x: "unharmed, not injured, undefiled," c. 1200, unmerred, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of mar (v.).

unneeded.x: "unnecessary, not required," 1725, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of need (v.). Unneedful in the same sense is from late 14c.

unperson.x: 1949 (Orwell), "person whose existence is officially ignored or denied as political punishment," from un- (1) "not" + person (n.).

unpicked.x: "not chosen or selected," 1580s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of pick (v.).

unprison.x: late 14c., unprisonen, "release or deliver from prison," from un- (2) "reverse of" + prison (v.). Related: Unprisoned; unprisoning.

unproved.x: "not demonstrated to be true; untested, not known by trial or established by argument," mid-15c., from un- (1) "not" + past participle of prove (v.). Unproven is attested by 1853. Middle English also had a verb unprove "disapprove of;" also "disprove, demonstrate the falseness of."

unreason.x: early 14c., unresoun, "lack of reason, irrationality; an injury, that which is unjustifiable;" from un- (1) "not" + reason (n.). By 1827 (Carlyle) as "absence of reason." The Abbot of Unreason of the Scottish revels is attested from late 15c.

unriddle.x: "explain or tell something to; solve or explain" what is mysterious, "interpret," 1580s, from un- (2) "reverse, opposite of" + riddle (v.2). Related: Unriddled; unriddling; unriddler.

unroofed.x: "not having a roof, deprived of a roof," 1640s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of roof (v.).

unsalted.x: "lacking salt, not having been salted or pickled, fresh," early 15c., from un- (1) "not" + past participle of salt (v.). Similar formation in North Frisian unsalted, Swedish osaltad, Danish usaltet.

unsecure.x: 1630s, from un- (1) "not" + secure (adj.). A useful word since insecure acquired a psychological sense but reported "obsolete" in OED (1989). The older form of the word was Middle English unsiker, "frail, weak; lacking confidence; not certain in mind," corresponding to German unsicher, from the nativized form of secure (adj.).

unserved.x: "not served" in any sense, mid-14c., from un- (1) "not" + past participle of serve (v.).

unsettle.x: 1590s, "undo from a fixed position, change from a settled state," from un- (2) "reverse, opposite of" + settle (v.). In reference to the mind, feelings, intellect, etc., it is attested from 1640s. Related: Unsettled; unsettling.

unshaken.x: mid-15c., "not agitated," from un- (1) "not" + shaken. The meaning "not moved from a firm position" is recorded from 1540s.

unshaven.x: "not shaven or trimmed," late 14c., from un- (1) "not" + past participle of shave (v.).

unsolved.x: "not explained or cleared up," 1660s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of solve (v.). Related: Unsolvable "insoluble" (1680s).

unsorted.x: "not arranged or put in order," 1530s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of sort (v.).

unsought.x: c. 1200, "not looked for or searched after;" c. 1300, "not asked for," late 14c., "not attempted;" from un- (1) "not" + past participle of seek (v.). Similar formation in Middle Dutch ongesocht, Dutch ongezocht, Middle High German ungesuochet, German ungesucht.

unspoken.x: early 15c., "omitted from utterance, passed over in speech," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of speak (v.). Similar formation in Middle Dutch ongesproken, Middle Low German ungesproken.

unsteady.x: 1590s, "not firm or secure in position," from un- (1) "not" + steady (adj.). The meaning "marked by irregularity" is from 1680s. Related: Unsteadily (1550s). Similar formation in Old Frisian unstadich, German unstätig, Middle Dutch onstadich. An earlier word in English was unsteadfast (Old English unstedfæst), typically of persons, faith, character. Also unstaþolfæst.
"make unsteady, cause to wobble," 1530s, from un- (2) "reverse, opposite of" + steady (v.). Related: Unsteadied; unsteadying.

unstring.x: 1610s, "deprive of strings; relax or untune the strings of." of a bow, lyre, etc., from un- (2) "reverse, opposite of" + string (v.). As "take (beads, etc.) from a string," 1690s; the general sense of "relax the tension of, render lax" is from c. 1700. Related: Unstringing; unstrung.

unstrung.x: 1590s, "with strings relaxed" (of a harp, etc.), from un- (1) "not" + past participle of string (v.). The transferred sense of "weakened, unnerved" is recorded from 1690s.

unsubtle.x: "not subtle" in any sense, c. 1500, from un- (1) "not" + subtle (adj.).

unsuited.x: "unfit, not adapted," 1590s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of suit (v.).

unswayed.x: "not biased, controlled, or influenced," 1590s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of sway (v.).

untangle.x: 1540s, "loosen from tangles," hence "clear up, free from doubt or uncertainty" (c. 1600); from un- (2) "reverse, opposite of" + tangle (v.). Related: Untangled; untangling.

untapped.x: 1680s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of tap (v.). Figurative use is by 1890.

untaught.x: late 14c., of a person, "not instructed or educated; without moral or spiritual guidance; unmannerly;" also as a noun, "untaught persons;" from un- (1) "not" + taught. Hence "spontaneous, uncommunicated by teaching" (mid-15c.). Also from mid-15c. in reference to intellectual topics, "unexamined and discussed."

untether.x: "release from a tether," 1775, from un- (2) "reverse, opposite of" + tether (v.). Related: Untethered; untethering.

untimely.x:
c. 1200, untimeli, "done at an inappropriate time;" 1530s, "coming before the proper or usual time;" from un- (1) "not" + timely (adj.).
Old English had untidlic "unseasonable" (see tide (n.)). Related: Untimeliness. Untime (n.) "unseasonable time; bad times, unfortunate conditions" is from Old English untima. Untimeous (adj.) is attested from c. 1500. Similar formation in Middle Danish utimelig, of weather, etc.

unturned.x: "not turned" in any sense, 1540s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of turn (v.).

unwalled.x: "not having walls," mid-15c., from un- (1) "not" + past participle of verb from wall (n.).

unwashed.x: "not cleansed by water," late 14c., from un- (1) "not" + past participle of wash (v.). Earlier was unwashen, from Old English unwæscen. The noun sense of "the lower class" (also great unwashed) is attested by 1830.

unweaned.x: "not yet weaned," literally or figuratively, 1580s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of wean (v.).

unworked.x: c. 1400, unwerked, of metal, "not shaped or beaten into form," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of work (v.).

unworthy.x:
mid-13c., unwurði, "deficient in worth, having no value;" of persons, "not deserving, wanting merit;" from un- (1) "not" + worthy (adj.). The meaning "beneath the character" of is by 1690s.
Similar formation in Middle Dutch onwerdich, Dutch onwaardig, Middle Low German unwerdich, Old High German unwirdig, Old Norse uverðugr. Old English had unweorðlic. Related: Unworthiness.

up-front.x: also upfront, 1975, "paid in advance;" 1977, "honest, open," from up front "in the front" (1932), from up + front (n.).

upgather.x: also up-gather, "gather up or together," 1580s, from verbal phrase, from up (adv.) + gather (v.). Related: Upgathered; upgathering.

upheaval.x: "a heaving or lifting up," 1834 in reference to convulsions in society; 1836 in reference to raised landforms in geology. With -al (2) + archaic verb upheave "rise up, arise; be elevated or exalted," from Old English uphebban; see up (adv.) + heave (v.). Similarly formed verbs are Old Frisian upheva, Old High German ufhevan, German aufheben.

uppercut.x:
in pugilism, a close-in strike upward with the fist, 1831, from upper (adj.) + cut (n.). Perhaps the image is of the action in chopping a tree by making cuts up (as well as down) in the trunk.
 It was on a side hill, and I observed a boy, who appeared to be about fifteen years of age, opposite the house felling a large tree; he had cut a few chips from the under side, and was then making the principal incision on the upper. ... I said to the boy, "Well Sir, I see that you make the upper cut." "That is the true cut," said the boy; "for if you will take the axe and try below, you will find that the tree will crowd down upon your chips, and you can't get it down in double the time." [Theodore Sedgwick, "Hints to My Countrymen," 1826]

urbanity.x: late 15c., "proper court behavior; courtesy of manners acquired by associating with well-bred people;" from Latin urbanitatem (nominative urbanitas) "city life; life in Rome; refinement, city fashion or manners, elegance, courtesy," also "wit, raillery, trickery," from urbanus "belonging to a city" (see urban (adj.)). Old French urbanité (14c.) was "city government."

urbanize.x: 1640s, "make more civil;" 1884 "make into a city," from urban + -ize; in the latter sense it is from French urbaniser (1873). By 1948 as "accustom to city life." Related: Urbanized; urbanizing.

urethane.x: 1838, in chemistry, from French uréthane (1833), coined by French chemist Jean-Baptiste Dumas, apparently from urea + ether + -ane as a generic chemical suffix.

untwist.x: "open or separate after having been twisted" (transitive), 1530s, from un- (2) "reverse, opposite of" + twist (v.). Intransitive sense by 1580s. The older word is untwine (late 14c.). Related: Untwisted; untwisting.

uliginous.x: "slimy, water-logged, oozy by nature," 1570s, from Latin uliginosus "full of moisture, poorly drained," from uligo "moisture, marshiness," a derivative of umere "be wet, moist" (see humid). Earlier was uliginose (mid-15c.).

ululation.x: "howling," as of a wolf or dog, 1590s, from Latin ululationem (nominative ululatio) "a howling or wailing," noun of action from past-participle stem of ululare "to howl, yell, shriek, wail, lament loudly," from a reduplicated imitative root (compare Greek ololyzein "to cry aloud," Sanskrit ululih "a howling," Lithuanian uliuoti "to howl," Gaelic uileliugh "wail of lamentation," Old English ule "owl").

umbilical.x: "pertaining to the navel; formed or placed like a navel," 1540s, from Medieval Latin umbilicalis "of the navel," from Latin umbilicus "navel" (see umbilicus). Umbilical cord attested by 1753 (a native term is navel string). Related: Umbilically.

unadorned.x: "not decorated, not embellished," 1630s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of adorn (v.).

unamiable.x: "repelling kind advances, not inducing love," 1771, from un- (1) "not" + amenable.

unapparel.x: "uncover, undress," 1570s, from un- (1) "not" + apparel (v.). Related: Unapparelled.

unbeknown.x: "unknown," 1630s, with to, from un- (1) "not" + beknown, past participle of beknow. Middle English had past-participle adjective unbiknowen (c. 1200). Compare unbeknownst.

unbounded.x: 1590s, "not limited in extent," often with a suggestion of "uncontrolled, unchecked," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of bound (v.1). The sense of "generous, profuse, liberal, immeasurably great" is recorded from 1704. Related: Unboundedness.

unceasing.x: late 14c., uncesinge, "never-ending, continual, not intermittent," from un- (1) "not" + present participle of cease (v.). Related: Unceasingly (mid-14c.).

unchanged.x: "not altered, unvaried," late 14c., unchaunged, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of change (v.).

uncharted.x: "not on a map or chart, of which there is no map or chart," 1804, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of chart (v.).

uncleanly.x: Middle English unclenli, "sinful, immoral, impure," from Old English unclænlic; see un- (1) "not" + cleanly (adj.), or perhaps unclean + -ly (1). Related: Uncleanliness.

uncleared.x: 1630s in reference to debts, by 1724 of imputations of guilt, 1772 in reference to land; from un- (1) "not" + past participle of clear (v.).

unclouded.x: "not obscured or darkened," 1590s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of cloud (v.). Figurative use by 1640s.

uncolored.x: also uncoloured, 1530s, "not stained or dyed," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of color (v.). By 1580s as "not having a specious or deceptive appearance, not biased in description." As a verb, uncolor is recorded from early 15c., "deprive of color, remove color from."

unconcern.x: "absence of anxiety, indifference," 1711, from un- (1) "not" + concern (n.).

uncounted.x: "not numbered," hence "innumerable," c. 1500, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of count (v.).

uncropped.x: c. 1600, "not plucked," of flowers, etc., from un- (1) "not" + past participle of crop (v.).

uncurable.x: "beyond the power or skill of medicine," mid-14c., from un- (1) "not" + curable.

uncurious.x: 1560s, "not inquisitive, wanting in curiosity," from un- (1) "not" + curious (adj.). From 1680s as "not odd or strange." Related: Uncuriously.

undeceive.x: "to free from deception or false belief, open one's eyes" to fallacy or error, 1590s, from un- (2) "opposite of" + deceive (v.). Related: Undeceived (c. 1400); undeceiving; undeceivable (c. 1400, "not false, trustworthy").

undefiled.x: mid-14c., undefilde, undefylde, "spiritually or morally pure, sinless, uncorrupted," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of defile (v.). Originally of clean morals generally; sense of "virginal, not sexually experienced" is attested from mid-15c. The physical sense of "not made dirty" is from 1580s.

underbred.x: "of inferior breeding, vulgar," 1640s, from under + past participle of breed (v.). In reference to animals, "not pure bred," by 1890.

underdone.x:
1680s, in reference to meat not entirely cooked; see under + done.
It likely was a past-participle adjective from underdo in its sense of "refrain from full action; "act below one's abilities" (early 17c.), especially "do less thoroughly than is requisite" (1716).
Earlier still, underdo (Old English underdon) meant "put under, subject, subjugate" and glossed Latin subigo. In Middle English to be underdone meant to be under one's gaze.

underfoot.x:
c. 1200, underfot "under the feet, on the ground, trodden on," figuratively "subservient, subjugated, vanquished;" from under + foot (n.). Compare similarly formed Middle Dutch ondervoete.
As an adjective, attested from 1590s, "low, base; abject, downtrodden," in reference to persons. As "continually in the way," it is recorded from 1891.

underpass.x: "part of a road running beneath another road or railroad," 1904, American English, from under + pass (n.).

underplay.x: 1850, in cards, "play a low card while holding a high one in hopes of later advantage," from under + play (v.). It is attested by 1896 in theater, "act a part with deliberate restraint." The figurative sense of "play down the importance of" is by 1949.

underrate.x: also under-rate, "esteem at too little worth, undervalue, rate below the true value," 1640s, from under + rate (v.). Related: Underrated; underrating.

undiluted.x: 1756, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of dilute (v.).

undivided.x: "not separated into parts or sections; whole; unanimous," early 15c., from un- (1) "not" + past participle of divide (v.). Related: Undividedly.

undoubted.x: "not called into question," of conditions, persons, authority, etc., mid-15c., undouted, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of doubt (v.). Related: Undoubtedly. Middle English also used undoutous "certain, sure," undouteful "steadfast, certain."

undreamed.x: also undreamt, "not dreamed, not imagined," hence "not thought of;" 1610s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of dream (v.).

unelected.x: "not elected, unchosen," 1580s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of elect (v.).

unequaled.x: also unequalled, "unparalleled, unrivaled," 1620s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of parallel (v.).

unfortune.x: "misfortune, bad luck" (archaic), early 15c., from un- (1) "not" + fortune (n.).

unfounded.x: 1640s, "having no foundation or basis," hence, in figurative use, "vain, idle; groundless, unwarranted;" from un- (1) "not" + past participle of found (v.1). Middle English verb unfound (mid-15c.) meant "destroy (a foundation)."

unguarded.x: 1590s, "not furnished with a guard," from un- (1) "not" + guarded. The sense of "not on one's guard, careless, not taking heed" is attested from 1630s. A verb unguard "deprive of a guard" is in Florio (1598).

unhappily.x: late 14c., "by ill fortune, unluckily;" early 15c., "wretchedly, without happiness," from un- (1) "not" + happily, or from unhappy + -ly (2.). Similar formation in Old Norse unheppiliga. It is attested by 1530s as "not suitably or appropriately." In parenthetical use, "regrettably," by 1580s.

unharness.x: c. 1400, unharneisen, "divest of armor," from un- (2) "opposite of" + harness (v.). Similar formation in Dutch ontharnassen "to disarm." The meaning "to free (a horse) from harness" is recorded from 1610s. Related: Unharnessed; unharnessing.

unhealthy.x: 1590s, "injurious to health," from un- (1) "not" + healthy (adj.). Earlier unhealthsome (1540s), unhealthful (1570s). Of persons, "sickly, lacking health, without vigor of growth," it is attested from 1610s. In World War I military slang, "dangerous." Related: Unhealthily; unhealthiness. Middle English had unhealth (n.) "unhealthiness, ill-health, disease," from Old English unhælþ.

unhelpful.x: "affording no aid," 1590s, from un- (1) "not" + helpful. Related: Unhelpfully; unhelpfulness. Earlier was unhelply (c. 1400). A noun unhelp "lack of help, hindrance" is attested by mid-15c.

unhonored.x: 1510s, also unhonoured, "not regarded with veneration," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of honor (v.). A verb unhonor "dishonor, mock" is attested from late 13c.

unimpeded.x: 1760, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of impede (v.).

uninjured.x: "having suffered no harm," 1570s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of injure (v.).

uninvited.x: "not having been invited," 1630s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of invite (v.).

unisexual.x: 1802, "of one sex, having only one sex," from uni- + sexual. Originally in botany; the meaning "of or for a single sex" (in reference to schools, etc.) is by 1885. The meaning "unisex, sexually indistinguishable" is attested by 1970. Related: Unisexual; unisexuality.

unknowing.x:
c. 1300, "without knowledge, ignorant," from un- (1) "not" + present participle of know (v.).
As a verbal noun meaning "ignorance, lack of knowledge, absence of awareness; incomprehension; uncertainty," it is recorded by mid-14c., especially in phrase cloud of unknowing, also title of a book of Christian mysticism in which unknowing meant something like "abandonment of knowledge the better to experience God, desire for transcendence of knowledge." Related: Unknowingly. A rare verb unknow "fail to recognize; become ignorant of" is attested from late 14c.

unlearned.x: late 14c., unlerned, "ignorant," from un- (1) "not" + learned (adj.). It is attested by 1530s as "not acquired by learning," from past participle of learn (v.). Old English had unlæred, Middle English unlered "unlearned, uninstructed, ignorant," from lere (v.). Related: Unlearnt.

unmanaged.x: "not controlled, regulated, or restrained," of a horse, "not broken in;" c. 1600, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of manage (v.).

unmarried.x: c. 1300, "refused a dower;" c. 1400, "not married;" from un- (1) "not" + past participle of marry (v.). In former use most often applied to one who has never married. A verb unmarry "divorce" is attested from 1520s.

unmeaning.x: "having no signification; not indicating intelligence," 1709, from un- (1) "not" + present participle of mean (v.). Related: Unmeaningly; unmeaningness.

unmindful.x: late 14c., unmindeful, "forgetful, heedless, inattentive," from un- (1) "not" + mindful (adj.). Unmind (adj.) in the same sense is attested from early 14c. Related: Unmindfully; unmindfulness.

unmuscled.x: "flaccid, having the muscles relaxed," 1748, from un- (1) "not" + verb from muscle (n.).

unnatural.x: late 14c., "abnormal, not in accord with physical nature," from un- (1) "not" + natural (adj.). The meaning "at variance with moral standards" is attested by 1520s; that of "unusual, strange, at variance with what is expected" is by 1580s. The sense of "artificial" is from 1746. Related: Unnaturally; unnaturalness.

unnoticed.x: "not observed or regarded," 1720, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of notice (v.).

unopposed.x: "not resisted, not meeting obstruction," 1650s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of oppose (v.).

unpainted.x: "not painted," late 15c., unpeinted, from un- (1) "not" + painted.

unplanned.x: "not planned," by 1804, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of plan (v.).

unpledged.x: "not pledged" in any sense, c. 1600, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of pledge (v.).

unpopular.x: "not having the public favor," 1640s, from un- (1) "not" + popular (adj.). Related: Unpopularly. Less common impopular is attested from 1721.

unreality.x: "lack of reality or existence," 1751, from un- (1) "not" + reality (n.). Unrealism is attested by 1859.

unrealize.x: 1804 (Southey), "make unreal;" see unreal + -ize. Unrealizable "incapable of being realized" is by 1840 (Carlyle).

unsettled.x: 1590s, "not peaceful, disturbed, lawless; not firmly established, not fixed in resolution," past-participle adjective from unsettle (v.); or else from un- (1) "not" + past participle of settle (v.). The meaning "not occupied by settlers, having no inhabitants" is attested from 1724. Related: Unsettledness.

unshriven.x: "unconfessed, not having been absolved of sins by the sacrament of penance," c. 1200, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of shrive (v.).

unskilled.x: 1580s, "lacking skill, not characterized by trained dexterity," from un- (1) "not" + skill. Unskilled labor is by 1833, "labor not requiring special skill or training," generally used of the simpler forms of manual labor.

unsmiling.x: 1730, from un- (1) "not" + present participle of smile (v.).
