unsparing.x: "showing no mercy," 1580s, from un- (1) "not" + sparing, which is attested from late 14c. as a present-participle adjective from spare (v.). The meaning "profuse" is from 1660s. Related: Unsparingly. Middle English had an adverb unsparely "without restraint" (c, 1200).

unspotted.x: late 14c., "untainted by sin, chaste, pure," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of spot (v.).

unstinted.x: late 15c., from un- (1) "not" + past participle of stint (v.).

unstudied.x: c. 1400, "not made a subject of study," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of study (v.). From 1650s as "natural, not artificial, not the result of study."

untainted.x: 1580s, of persons, "not morally impure;" c. 1600 in the physical sense, "not sullied, unblemished;" from un- (1) "not" + past participle of taint (v.). Earlier adjective was untained (mid-15c.), from a Middle English variant of taint (v.). Related: Untaintable (c. 1600).

unthought.x: mid-15c., "not imagined or conceived," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of think (v.). A verb unthink "retract in thought, remove from the mind or thoughts" is attested from c. 1600.

unthrifty.x: late 14c., unthrifti, "unprofitable, useless; evil, wicked;" by 1530s as "not careful with one's means;" from un- (1) "not" + thrifty (adj.), or else from Middle English noun unthrift "profligacy" (late 14c.). This noun also meant "evil practice, wicked act" (c. 1300), also "a prodigal, one who wastes his estate" (early 14c.). Related: Unthriftily; unthriftiness.

untrained.x: "not disciplined, uneducated," 1540s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of train (v.).

untrodden.x: c. 1400, of a path, "not walked upon, not passed over, unfrequented," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of tread (v.).

unwearied.x: "not fatigued," c. 1200, unweried, from Old English ungewerigod; see un- (1) "not" + weary (v.). Related: Unweary (Old English unwerig).

unwilling.x: "loath, disinclined, reluctant," early 15c., an altered form of Middle English unwilland, from Old English unwillende; or else a new formation from un- (1) "not" + willing (adj.). Also see -ing (2). Related: Unwillingly; unwillingness.

unwomanly.x: "not in the manner of a woman, in a manner unbecoming to a woman," early 15c.; see un- (1) "not" + woman + -ly (2).

unworldly.x: 1707, "transcending what is mundane or of the Earth," from un- (1) "not" + worldly (adj.). Of persons, "spiritual, not influenced by sordid matters," by 1825. Related: Unworldliness.

unwritten.x:
late 14c., "unrecorded, not reduced to writing, oral, traditional," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of write (v.). By mid-15c. as "not distinctly laid down but generally understood."
 Unwritten law, law which, although it may be reduced to writing, rests for its authority on custom or judicial decision, etc., as distinguished from law originating in written command, statute, or decree. [Century Dictionary] 
 Similar formation in Old English unwriten, Old Norse uritinn.

uppermost.x: mid-15c., uppermoste, "highest, in or to the highest or most elevated place or position; of or pertaining to the top or highest part," from upper (adj.) + -most. Middle English also had uppermore; Chaucer uses upperest.

upwelling.x: 1841, from up (adv.) + present participle of well (v.). As a noun from 1847. A verb upwell is attested from 1885, "issue forth" as water from a fountain. It was used earlier as "to spit up, vomit" (Old English upweallan).

urceolate.x: "shaped like a pitcher, urn-shaped," especially in botany, 1760, with -ate (1) + Latin urceolus "little pitcher," diminutive of urceus "pitcher," a word of uncertain origin (see urn).

urticaria.x: "nettle-rash, hives," medical Latin, from Latin urtica "nettle, stinging nettle" (figuratively "spur, incentive, stimulant), from urere "to burn" (from PIE root *eus- "to burn;" see ember) + abstract noun ending -ia. Related: Urticarial; urticarious.

uttermost.x: "farthest, remotest," late 14c., outremost, from utter (adj.) + -most. More recent than utmost (q.v.). As a noun, "farthest point, extremity," late 14c. Middle English had also uttermore (late 14c.) also utterest (c. 1200), also used as a noun, "extreme end."
